abbey_cocktail.description: The Abbey is a cocktail from "The Savoy Cocktail Book": gin, Lillet, orange juice and a dash of bitters. Pale, citrusy and very much an aperitif, it is a relative of the Bronx but softer thanks to the wine.

absinthe_drip.instructions: Place a sugar cube on a special spoon over a glass of absinthe and slowly drip ice-cold water over it until the absinthe turns cloudy.
absinthe_drip.description: The traditional French ritual of the 'green hour' in 19th-century cafés. Ice-cold water dripping slowly through sugar on a slotted spoon makes the absinthe turn cloudy (the louche): anise and fennel essential oils come out of solution as an emulsion, releasing the aroma. Absinthe was banned in France and many other countries from 1910–15 until the early 21st century.

absinthe_frappe.instructions: Shake the absinthe, syrup and water with ice and pour over crushed ice.
absinthe_frappe.description: The Absinthe Frappé was created by Cayetano Ferrer in 1874 at the New Orleans bar later known as the Old Absinthe House. In the late 19th century the drink was so popular that it was even sung about in a Broadway operetta. Absinthe, sugar and crushed ice make a refreshing anise alternative to the traditional drip service.
absinthe_frappe.creator: Cayetano Ferrer (Old Absinthe House)

adonis.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
adonis.description: The Adonis was created in New York in 1884 in honour of the Broadway musical Adonis, the first show to run more than 500 performances. Fino sherry and sweet vermouth make it a softer, sweeter sibling of the Bamboo. It is one of the best low-ABV aperitifs of the 19th century and a great match for olives and jamón.
adonis.creator: Waldorf Hotel bar

affinity.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
affinity.description: The Affinity is a 'perfect' Rob Roy in equal parts: Scotch and two vermouths. The recipe dates to the early 20th century and appears in The Savoy Cocktail Book. A light, aromatic aperitif in which the vermouths stand on equal footing with the whisky.

agua_de_jamaica.instructions: Pour hot water over the hibiscus, steep, strain, sweeten and chill.
agua_de_jamaica.description: Agua de Jamaica is a Mexican agua fresca made from hibiscus flowers, bright ruby and tart, similar to cranberry mors. It is served in every taquería; in Russia a similar drink is known as cold karkade.

agua_de_valencia.instructions: Mix in a pitcher with ice and pour into glasses.
agua_de_valencia.description: Agua de Valencia was created by Constante Gil in 1959 at Café Madrid in Valencia — according to legend, for Basque visitors tired of the local 'water' (as cava was called). Valencian oranges, cava and a little vodka and gin make a festive pitcher drink.
agua_de_valencia.creator: Constante Gil (Café Madrid)

air_mail.instructions: Shake the rum, lime and honey with ice, strain into the glass and top up with champagne.
air_mail.description: The Air Mail was first described in "Esquire's Handbook for Hosts" (1949), though its roots are probably Cuban. It can be described as a rum French 75 with honey or as a sparkling Canchánchara. The name nods to airmail, fashionable at the time; some bars serve it garnished with an envelope or a stamp.

alabama_slammer.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over ice (or serve as shots).
alabama_slammer.description: The Alabama Slammer is a 1970s college-party cocktail associated with the University of Alabama. Southern Comfort, amaretto and sloe gin with orange juice — sweet, fruity and sneaky; it is served both in a tall glass and as shots.

alaska.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
alaska.description: The Alaska appears in early-20th-century American books and in The Savoy Cocktail Book, where Craddock wryly notes that it was apparently not invented in Alaska. Yellow Chartreuse, softer and more honeyed than green, takes the place of vermouth in a Martini template. The result is dry yet aromatic and herbal.

algarrobina.instructions: Blend with ice and dust with cinnamon.
algarrobina.description: The Algarrobina is a Peruvian dessert cocktail made with pisco and syrup from the pods of the carob-like algarrobo tree, whose flavor recalls caramel and cocoa. With milk and egg yolk it becomes a thick, sweet flip.

algonquin.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
algonquin.description: Named after New York's Algonquin Hotel, where Dorothy Parker's famous literary Round Table gathered in the 1920s. Rye whiskey, dry vermouth and pineapple make an unusual but balanced combination: spicy, dry and slightly tropical.

amaretto_sour.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice; strain over fresh ice.
amaretto_sour.description: The Amaretto Sour became popular in the US in the 1970s on the back of amaretto marketing and for years was made with bottled sour mix. Its reputation was rescued in 2012 by Portland bartender Jeffrey Morgenthaler, who added bourbon, fresh lemon and egg white: the sweetness came into balance and the almond flavor gained depth. It is one of the best options for those who don't like strong drinks.

americano.instructions: Pour the Campari and vermouth over ice, top up with soda and stir gently.
americano.description: The Americano grew out of the Milano-Torino, a mix of Milanese Campari and Turin vermouth served at Gaspare Campari's bar in the 1860s. Later it was lengthened with soda, and the name, according to the popular story, comes from American tourists of the Prohibition era who fell for the drink. It is the direct ancestor of the Negroni and one of the best light aperitifs: bittersweet, refreshing and not too strong. It is the first cocktail James Bond orders in Fleming's Casino Royale.
americano.creator: Gaspare Campari (Caffè Campari)

ancient_mariner.instructions: Shake with ice and pour over crushed ice.
ancient_mariner.description: Jeff Berry, tiki's foremost historian, created the Ancient Mariner in 1994, inspired by old Donn Beach recipes. Two rums, lime, grapefruit and allspice dram make a spiced, balanced tiki drink. The name comes from Coleridge's poem.
ancient_mariner.creator: Jeff "Beachbum" Berry

angel_face.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
angel_face.description: A recipe from Harry Craddock's "The Savoy Cocktail Book" (1930) with three equal parts: gin, apricot liqueur and calvados. Despite the lack of citrus, the cocktail isn't cloying: the apple brandy and gin provide a dry backbone, while the apricot adds soft fruitiness. A good autumn digestif and an example of the spirit-forward cocktails of the interwar era.
angel_face.creator: Harry Craddock

aperol_sour.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain.
aperol_sour.description: The Aperol Sour is a modern sour built on the Italian orange bitter aperitif: bittersweet orange, tart and with a fluffy foam. A good low-ABV alternative to a Pisco or Whiskey Sour, popularized by the brand itself.

aperol_spritz.instructions: Fill a glass with ice, pour in the prosecco, then the Aperol, top up with soda and stir gently.
aperol_spritz.description: The spritz tradition goes back to 19th-century Austrian soldiers in the Veneto who diluted the local wine with water (spritzen means "to splash"). Aperol was created by the Barbieri brothers in Padua in 1919, and the modern 3-2-1 recipe was heavily promoted by the brand from the 1950s onward, especially in the 2000s, when the Aperol Spritz became a summer symbol across Europe. Bright orange, bittersweet and low in alcohol, it's the perfect aperitif.

appletini.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
appletini.description: The Appletini (or Apple Martini) appeared in 1996 at Lola's in West Hollywood, where bartender Adam Karsten was experimenting with apple schnapps. Bright green and sweet-and-sour, it became a symbol of the late-'90s and 2000s "-tini" craze; J.D. often drinks it on the TV series Scrubs.
appletini.creator: Adam Karsten (Lola's)

army_and_navy.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
army_and_navy.description: The cocktail is described in David Embury's The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks (1948); the name probably refers to the annual Army–Navy football game. It is a gin sour with almond orgeat in place of sugar, making for a soft, velvety, aromatic drink.

arnold_palmer.instructions: Pour iced tea and lemonade half and half into a glass over ice.
arnold_palmer.description: The drink is named after legendary golfer Arnold Palmer, who liked to mix iced tea with lemonade and ordered it at clubs in the 1960s. Simple, refreshing and not too sweet; with vodka it is called a John Daly.
arnold_palmer.creator: Arnold Palmer

art_of_choke.instructions: Stir with ice and strain over ice.
art_of_choke.description: Kyle Davidson created the Art of Choke at The Violet Hour in Chicago: the artichoke amaro Cynar paired with rum and Chartreuse, stirred with mint and a dash of lime. The name is a pun on 'art' and artichoke. Bitter, herbal and complex.
art_of_choke.creator: Kyle Davidson (The Violet Hour)

aviation.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
aviation.description: The recipe was published in 1916 by Hugo Ensslin, bartender at New York's Hotel Wallick, at the height of the aviation craze. Violet liqueur gives the drink its sky-lilac color, but it eventually vanished from the market, and for decades the Aviation was made without it. Since crème de violette returned in 2007, the cocktail has regained its hue and floral aroma.
aviation.creator: Hugo Ensslin (Hotel Wallick)

b52.instructions: Layer over a bar spoon in this order: coffee liqueur, cream liqueur, orange liqueur. Sometimes set alight.
b52.description: The layered B-52 shot appeared in the late 1970s; one version of its origin ties it to Peter Fich, a bartender at the Keg restaurant in Banff, Canada. It is named either after the strategic bomber or after the rock band The B-52's. Three liqueurs of different densities settle into neat layers, and the top orange layer is sometimes set on fire.
b52.creator: Peter Fich (Keg Steakhouse, according to one version)

b53.instructions: Layer one bar spoon at a time: coffee liqueur, sambuca, orange liqueur.
b53.description: The B-53 is a variation on the B-52 with sambuca in place of the cream liqueur. The result is a stronger, aniseed-forward layered shot; as with the B-52, the top layer is sometimes set alight.

b_and_b.instructions: Pour into a glass and stir gently (serve without ice).
b_and_b.description: B&B is a mix of brandy and Bénédictine that, according to the common version, was invented at New York's 21 Club in the 1930s. The drink proved so popular that the Bénédictine producer has sold it ready-bottled since 1938. A classic digestif.
b_and_b.creator: 21 Club (according to legend)

baby_guinness.instructions: Pour the coffee liqueur and carefully float a "head" of cream liqueur on top.
baby_guinness.description: This shot looks like a miniature pint of Guinness: dark coffee liqueur below and a white creamy "head" on top. Popular in Irish pubs around the world, especially on St. Patrick's Day.

bacardi_cocktail.description: The Bacardi is a pink Daiquiri with grenadine. In 1936 the New York State Supreme Court ruled that this cocktail could only be made with Bacardí rum — a rare case of a recipe protected by a court. Sweet-tart, fruity and simple.

bahama_mama.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a glass over ice.
bahama_mama.description: A resort rum punch from the Bahamas that became popular in the mid-20th century on the wave of the tiki craze. Coconut and dark rum, orange, pineapple and grenadine make a simple and very sweet drink. Every bar has its own recipe; some versions use coffee or banana liqueur.

bamboo.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
bamboo.description: The Bamboo is credited to Louis Eppinger, bartender at the Grand Hotel in Yokohama in the 1890s, who served foreigners in Meiji-era Japan. Dry sherry and dry vermouth with bitters make a light, saline, nutty aperitif. With the rise of interest in low-ABV drinks, it has enjoyed a real revival.
bamboo.creator: Louis Eppinger (Grand Hotel)

bandera.instructions: Serve three shot glasses (green: lime, white: tequila, red: sangrita) and sip from each in turn.
bandera.description: The Bandera ("flag") is a Mexican way of serving tequila in three shot glasses in the colors of the national flag: lime juice, tequila and spicy tomato-citrus sangrita. They're sipped in turn, alternating between them.

barracuda.instructions: Shake the rum, Galliano and juices with ice, strain into a glass and top up with prosecco.
barracuda.description: The Barracuda is an Italian cocktail from the 1960s credited to bartender Benito Cuppari. A rum base with pineapple and vanilla Galliano, livened up with sparkling wine, makes it light and festive. For a long time it was little known outside Italy, until it made the IBA list.
barracuda.creator: Benito Cuppari (according to one version)

bartenders_handshake.instructions: Drink a shot of Fernet and chase it with ginger beer.
bartenders_handshake.description: In San Francisco bars, a shot of Fernet with a ginger beer chaser is the unofficial "bartender's handshake", poured for fellow bartenders and regulars. Bitter, minty and herbal, it is considered a good digestif.

batanga.instructions: Rim the glass with salt, pour the tequila and juice over ice, top up with cola and stir (traditionally with a knife).
batanga.description: The Batanga was invented by Don Javier Delgado Corona in 1961 at La Capilla in the town of Tequila, one of Mexico's oldest bars. The name was a friend's nickname. The signature touch: Don Javier stirred the drink with the long knife he had just used to cut limes and other ingredients. Essentially it's a Mexican Cuba Libre with a salt rim.
batanga.creator: Don Javier Delgado Corona (La Capilla)

batida.description: The Batida (from the Portuguese for "beaten") is a Brazilian cocktail of cachaça, fruit and condensed milk. The most popular versions are passion fruit (batida de maracujá) and coconut (batida de coco). It is a creamy, sweet and very tropical drink sold on the beaches and in the bars of Rio.

beergarita.instructions: Build tequila, liqueur and lime over ice in a salt-rimmed glass and top up with beer (or upend a small bottle into the glass).
beergarita.description: The Beergarita is a Margarita lengthened with Mexican lager; bars often serve it with an upturned mini bottle of Coronita right in the glass. Lighter, fizzier and lower in alcohol than the classic.

bees_knees.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
bees_knees.description: The name is 1920s slang for "top notch" or "just the thing". The recipe is often credited to Frank Meier of the Paris Ritz, though there are also American Prohibition-era versions in which honey and lemon masked the taste of bathtub gin. Today it's a simple, elegant sour whose flavor depends heavily on the type of honey.
bees_knees.creator: Frank Meier (Ritz, by one account)

bellini.instructions: Pour the peach purée into a chilled glass, slowly top up with prosecco and stir gently.
bellini.description: Giuseppe Cipriani, founder of Harry's Bar in Venice, created the cocktail in 1948. Its delicate pink color reminded him of a saint's robe in a painting by Giovanni Bellini, whose exhibition was then on in Venice. The classic is made with white peach purée, pressed by hand at the bar when the fruit is in season.
bellini.creator: Giuseppe Cipriani (Harry's Bar)

bensonhurst.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
bensonhurst.description: Chad Solomon's 2006 twist on the Brooklyn cocktail, with Amer Picon swapped for the artichoke amaro Cynar. Dry, slightly bitter and herbal, it belongs to the renaissance-era series of New York "neighborhood" cocktails.
bensonhurst.creator: Chad Solomon

bentons_old_fashioned.instructions: Stir with ice and strain over a large cube.
bentons_old_fashioned.description: At the New York speakeasy PDT, Don Lee infused bourbon with the fat of Benton's smoked bacon and sweetened it with maple syrup. This cocktail is what made fat-washing popular: a smoky, salty "breakfast" Old Fashioned.
bentons_old_fashioned.creator: Don Lee (PDT)

bermuda_rum_swizzle.instructions: Combine in a pitcher or glass with crushed ice and swizzle with a swizzle stick until frothy and frosted.
bermuda_rum_swizzle.description: The Rum Swizzle is considered Bermuda's national drink, and the Swizzle Inn pub, opened in 1932, claims to be its birthplace. Traditionally it is made by the pitcher for a group and swizzled until frothy. Dark and gold rum with fruit juices and falernum make a festive tropical punch.
bermuda_rum_swizzle.creator: Swizzle Inn

between_the_sheets.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
between_the_sheets.description: A drink of the 1920s–30s attributed to Harry MacElhone of Harry's New York Bar in Paris; another version says it originated at the Berkeley Hotel in London. It is a Sidecar with half the cognac replaced by white rum. The provocative name was once a nod to its use as an "aperitif" in certain notorious Parisian establishments.
between_the_sheets.creator: Harry MacElhone (according to one version)

bicicletta.instructions: Pour the wine and Campari over ice and top up with soda.
bicicletta.description: The Bicicletta ("bicycle") is a Lombard aperitif of white wine, Campari and soda. According to legend, the name comes from old men who drank at the bar and then wobbled home on their bicycles. It's the great-grandfather of today's popular spritz.

biere_picon.instructions: Pour the Picon into a glass and top up with beer.
biere_picon.description: Picon Bière is a classic aperitif of northeastern France: lager with bittersweet orange Amer Picon. In the bars of Alsace and Lorraine it is ordered as naturally as a glass of beer.

bijou.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
bijou.description: The Bijou ("jewel") is credited to Harry Johnson, one of the first professional bartender-authors, who published the recipe in 1900. The name refers to the colors of the ingredients: gin is the diamond, vermouth the ruby, Chartreuse the emerald. It's a powerful herbal cocktail dominated by Chartreuse; many modern bartenders dial it back.
bijou.creator: Harry Johnson

bitter_french.instructions: Shake everything except the champagne, strain into a flute and top up with sparkling wine.
bitter_french.description: Phil Ward added a touch of Campari to the French 75, creating a pinkish, bittersweet sparkling aperitif. This simple change makes the classic drier and more grown-up. Great as a pre-dinner aperitif or a celebratory toast.
bitter_french.creator: Phil Ward

bitter_giuseppe.instructions: Stir with ice and strain over fresh ice.
bitter_giuseppe.description: Stephen Cole created the Bitter Giuseppe at The Violet Hour in Chicago, making artichoke amaro Cynar the base of the cocktail. It is an "inverted" Manhattan where the liqueur matters more than the spirit: bitter, herbal and yet low in alcohol.
bitter_giuseppe.creator: Stephen Cole (The Violet Hour)

bitter_mai_tai.instructions: Shake with ice and pour over crushed ice.
bitter_mai_tai.description: Jeremy Oertel made Campari the main spirit of the Mai Tai, with only half a measure of Jamaican rum. The result is a bright red, bitter and nutty tiki drink that became an example of the "bitter as base" idea popular in the 2010s.
bitter_mai_tai.creator: Jeremy Oertel (Dutch Kills)

black_and_tan.instructions: Pour the ale, then slowly pour the stout over an upturned spoon so it settles on top.
black_and_tan.description: A layered beer: pale ale on the bottom and dark stout on top (the stout is lighter thanks to nitrogen carbonation). Popular in British and American pubs; in Ireland the name is disliked because of its historical associations, and the drink goes by other names, such as Half and Half.

black_manhattan.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
black_manhattan.description: Todd Smith of San Francisco's Bourbon & Branch swapped the sweet vermouth in a Manhattan for the Sicilian amaro Averna. The result is a darker, bittersweet-caramel and herbal cocktail. It became one of the symbols of the amaro craze in American bars of the 2000s.
black_manhattan.creator: Todd Smith (Bourbon & Branch)

black_russian.instructions: Build in an ice-filled glass and stir.
black_russian.description: Gustave Tops, bartender at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels, created the drink in 1949 for Perle Mesta, the US ambassador to Luxembourg. The name nods to the dawning Cold War: "Russian" vodka and dark coffee liqueur. It's a simple, sweet digestif that spawned a whole family, including the White Russian and the Mudslide.
black_russian.creator: Gustave Tops (Hotel Metropole)

black_velvet.instructions: Fill the glass halfway with stout and slowly top up with champagne over a bar spoon.
black_velvet.description: The Black Velvet was created at Brooks's club in London in 1861, during the mourning for Prince Albert, when it was felt that even champagne should "wear mourning". Stout and champagne form a velvety mix with coffee and bready notes and a sparkling freshness. In Ireland it is often drunk at celebrations alongside oysters.
black_velvet.creator: Bartender at Brooks's Club

blackthorn.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
blackthorn.description: The name Blackthorn belongs to two different classic cocktails: an English one made with sloe gin and an Irish one made with Irish whiskey. The Irish version from The Savoy Cocktail Book — with dry vermouth, absinthe and bitters — is dry, aromatic and anise-tinged.

blinker.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
blinker.description: The Blinker appeared in Patrick Gavin Duffy's The Official Mixer's Manual (1934), where it was made with grenadine. Cocktail historian Ted Haigh, studying the recipe, suggested swapping the grenadine for raspberry syrup, and that is how it became popular. Rye whiskey, grapefruit and raspberry give it a tart, berry-driven and slightly bitter flavour.

blood_and_sand.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
blood_and_sand.description: The cocktail is named after the silent film Blood and Sand (1922), starring Rudolph Valentino as a bullfighter, and was first printed in "The Savoy Cocktail Book." The red cherry liqueur and orange juice symbolize the blood and sand of the arena. One of the few classic cocktails pairing Scotch with orange; sweet, fruity and smooth.

bloody_bull.instructions: Mix with ice by rolling between two glasses.
bloody_bull.description: A hybrid of the Bloody Mary and the Bullshot: tomato juice and beef broth in equal parts. Especially popular at New Orleans brunches (for example, at Brennan's). Richer and meatier than a classic Mary.

bloody_mary.instructions: Combine the ingredients with ice, roll between two tins a few times (do not shake) and serve over ice.
bloody_mary.description: Fernand Petiot claimed he mixed vodka with tomato juice in 1921 at Harry's New York Bar in Paris, and in 1934, working at New York's St. Regis hotel, added salt, pepper, lemon and Worcestershire sauce. The name is linked either to Queen Mary I Tudor or to a customer named Mary. It is the ultimate brunch and hangover cocktail, with countless regional variations — from Canada's Bloody Caesar with clam juice to the tequila-based Bloody Maria.
bloody_mary.creator: Fernand Petiot

blue_hawaii.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a glass with ice.
blue_hawaii.description: Harry Yee, the legendary bartender at Honolulu's Hilton Hawaiian Village, created the Blue Hawaii in 1957 at the request of a representative of a Dutch company promoting blue curaçao. The name stuck after the Elvis Presley film of the same name (1961). Not to be confused with the Blue Hawaiian, which also contains coconut cream.
blue_hawaii.creator: Harry Yee (Hilton Hawaiian Village)

blue_lagoon.instructions: Pour the vodka and liqueur into a glass with ice, top up with lemonade and stir.
blue_lagoon.description: The Blue Lagoon is usually credited to Andy MacElhone, son of the founder of Harry's New York Bar in Paris, around 1960, shortly after blue curaçao came on the market. Its vivid blue color made it a favorite of resort bars and parties. The flavor is simple: orange liqueur, lemon soda and vodka.
blue_lagoon.creator: Andy MacElhone (Harry's New York Bar)

bob_marley_shot.instructions: Layer in order: grenadine, crème de menthe, Galliano.
bob_marley_shot.description: A layered shot in the colors of the Rastafarian flag — red, green and yellow. There are several recipes (TheCocktailDB's uses Midori, Jägermeister and Goldschläger); the classic version is grenadine, crème de menthe and Galliano.

bobby_burns.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
bobby_burns.description: Named after the Scottish poet Robert Burns, this cocktail is traditionally served on 25 January, Burns Night. Essentially it is a Rob Roy with a few dashes of Bénédictine, which adds honeyed, herbal notes. The recipe dates to the early 20th century and appears in The Savoy Cocktail Book.

boilermaker.instructions: Serve a shot of whiskey alongside a beer, or drop the shot into the beer and drink.
boilermaker.description: The Boilermaker is an American working-class tradition: a shot of whiskey with a beer chaser. The name is linked to boilermakers, workers who stopped by the bar after a shift for a quick, cheap drink. Today many bars offer "boilermakers" as thoughtful pairings of a specific whiskey and beer style.

bombardino.instructions: Warm the liqueur with the brandy (do not boil), pour into a mug and top with whipped cream.
bombardino.description: The Bombardino is a hot drink from Italian ski resorts, said to come from Livigno in Lombardy. Its creator, warming up frozen skiers, mixed hot egg liqueur with brandy, and one guest exclaimed, "It's a bomb!" Creamy, warming and very rich, it's Italy's quintessential après-ski.

boulevardier.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass or over fresh ice.
boulevardier.description: The Boulevardier is the "whiskey Negroni," though it appeared at almost the same time as the Negroni itself. The recipe was first printed in Harry MacElhone's "Barflies and Cocktails" (1927) and credited to Erskine Gwynne, an American writer who published The Boulevardier magazine in Paris. Whiskey makes the drink warmer and rounder than a Negroni, which is why it's often recommended as an autumn and winter aperitif. Many bartenders raise the proportion of whiskey so the Campari's bitterness doesn't dominate.
boulevardier.creator: Erskine Gwynne

bourbon_renewal.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over fresh ice.
bourbon_renewal.description: Jeffrey Morgenthaler came up with the cocktail in the early 2000s when he found himself with a spare bottle of crème de cassis. The bourbon sour with cassis turned out berry-rich, bright and simple, and quickly became a modern classic.
bourbon_renewal.creator: Jeffrey Morgenthaler

boxcar.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain into a sugar-rimmed glass.
boxcar.description: The Boxcar is a relative of the White Lady with a spoonful of grenadine and a sugar rim, known from American bar guides (it is listed in TheCocktailDB). Pinkish, frothy and citrusy.

boyarsky.instructions: Pour the grenadine, layer the vodka on top over a bar spoon and add a dash of Tabasco.
boyarsky.description: A St. Petersburg shot named after actor Mikhail Boyarsky: red grenadine below and vodka on top, sometimes with a dash of Tabasco. Downed in one; popular in the bars of Rubinstein Street.

brain_hemorrhage.instructions: Pour the schnapps, slowly add the cream liqueur (it will curdle into 'brain folds') and add a few drops of grenadine.
brain_hemorrhage.description: A Halloween shot: cream liqueur curdles in peach schnapps into a 'brain', while drops of grenadine stand in for blood. It looks frightening but tastes sweet and fruity.

bramble.instructions: Shake the gin, juice and syrup with ice, strain over crushed ice and drizzle the blackberry liqueur over the top.
bramble.description: Dick Bradsell, one of the key figures of the 1980s London bar scene, created the Bramble in 1984 at Fred's Club in Soho, inspired by childhood memories of picking blackberries on the Isle of Wight. The liqueur poured on top slowly bleeds down through the ice, creating a striking gradient. Simple and thoroughly British in spirit, it quickly became a modern classic.
bramble.creator: Dick Bradsell (Fred's Club)

brancolada.instructions: Blend with crushed ice and pour into the glass.
brancolada.description: The Brancolada is a Piña Colada with mint fernet Branca Menta added. The bitter-minty amaro pairs surprisingly well with coconut and pineapple, making the cocktail refreshing and less cloying than the original.
brancolada.creator: Jeremy Oertel

brandy_alexander.instructions: Shake with ice, strain into a chilled glass and dust with nutmeg.
brandy_alexander.description: The original early-20th-century Alexander was made with gin; according to one version, it was created by bartender Troy Alexander at Rector's in New York for a dinner honoring Phoebe Snow, an advertising character dressed in white. Over time the cognac version became the standard. It is said to have been John Lennon's favorite cocktail. A classic dessert drink — creamy, chocolatey, with a nutmeg aroma.

brandy_cobbler.instructions: Briefly shake with the citrus, pour over crushed ice and garnish with fruit.
brandy_cobbler.description: 19th-century cobblers were spirits or wine with sugar and fruit over a mound of crushed ice. The brandy version sat alongside the Sherry Cobbler in bars of the Jerry Thomas era. Fruity and refreshing, but with a strong cognac backbone.

brandy_crusta.instructions: Rim the glass with sugar and line the inside with a spiral of peel; shake the ingredients with ice and strain.
brandy_crusta.description: Italian bartender Joseph Santini created the Crusta in the 1850s at his New Orleans bar, the Jewel of the South. It was one of the first cocktails to use citrus and is considered a direct ancestor of the Sidecar and the Margarita. The name means "crust", after the sugar rim, and the long spiral of lemon peel inside the glass makes for a striking presentation.
brandy_crusta.garnish: sugar rim, long lemon peel inside the glass
brandy_crusta.creator: Joseph Santini (Jewel of the South)

brandy_daisy.instructions: Shake with ice, strain over crushed ice and add soda.
brandy_daisy.description: The Brandy Daisy, from Jerry Thomas's 1876 book, is one of the first daisies and a direct ancestor of the Sidecar. Cognac, lemon and orange liqueur with a splash of soda — lively and fruity.
brandy_daisy.creator: Jerry Thomas

brandy_flip.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain; dust with nutmeg.
brandy_flip.description: A whole-egg flip is a classic 19th-century form described by Jerry Thomas. After a hard shake, cognac, sugar and egg give a thick, velvety drink similar to a cold eggnog.

brandy_milk_punch.instructions: Shake with ice, strain over fresh ice and dust with nutmeg.
brandy_milk_punch.description: Milk punches date back to the 17th century, but the Brandy Milk Punch became a classic of New Orleans brunch, especially at Brennan's. It is chilled milk with cognac, vanilla and nutmeg, tasting like a light eggnog without the egg. In the city it is traditionally drunk on weekend mornings and holidays.

brave_bull.instructions: Build in an ice-filled glass and stir.
brave_bull.description: The Brave Bull is the tequila sibling of the Black Russian, dating from the mid-20th century; the name plays on Mexican bullfighting. Tequila and coffee liqueur make a simple, sweet digestif in which agave's herbal notes set off the coffee. With cream it's called a Toro Bravo or "White Bull".

breakfast_martini.instructions: Stir the marmalade into the gin in a shaker, add the rest and ice, shake and double strain.
breakfast_martini.description: Salvatore Calabrese created this cocktail in 1996 at the Lanesborough hotel after his wife made him eat toast with orange marmalade at breakfast. A spoonful of bittersweet British marmalade turns a White Lady into a drink with a vivid citrus flavor. It is sometimes served with a small piece of toast on a pick.
breakfast_martini.creator: Salvatore Calabrese

bronx.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
bronx.description: Johnny Solon of New York's Waldorf-Astoria said he created the Bronx around 1900 and named it after the newly opened Bronx Zoo. In the 1930s the Bronx was one of America's most popular cocktails, second only to the Martini and the Manhattan. It is a Perfect Martini with orange juice: light, fruity and aperitif-style.
bronx.creator: Johnny Solon (Waldorf-Astoria)

brooklyn.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
brooklyn.description: The Brooklyn was first published by Jacob Grohusko in 1908 — the borough of Brooklyn's answer to the Manhattan. Dry vermouth replaces sweet, and Amer Picon, a bittersweet orange French aperitif, adds depth. Since Picon is hard to find, amaro is used instead; the Brooklyn became the model for a whole series of 'neighborhood' cocktails (Red Hook, Greenpoint, Bensonhurst).
brooklyn.creator: Jacob Grohusko

brown_derby.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
brown_derby.description: A 1930s cocktail from Hollywood's Vendôme Club, named after the famous Brown Derby restaurant, built in the shape of a bowler hat. Bourbon, grapefruit and honey make a simple, harmonious trio in which the grapefruit's bitterness balances the honey's sweetness. A close relative of the Gold Rush, though 70 years older.
brown_derby.creator: Vendôme Club

bullshot.instructions: Mix with ice, roll between tins several times and serve.
bullshot.description: The Bullshot appeared in the 1950s at the Caucus Club in Detroit as part of a marketing push for canned beef broth. Essentially it's a Bloody Mary with beef broth instead of tomato juice: rich, salty and savory. Popular with the brunch and hunting crowd; there's also a hot version.
bullshot.creator: Caucus Club

bushwacker.description: The Bushwacker was born in the 1970s on St. Thomas as an answer to the Piña Colada, and later became a cult drink of the Gulf Coast in Florida and Alabama. It is a boozy milkshake with rum, coffee and chocolate liqueurs and coconut.
bushwacker.creator: Ship's Store, St. Thomas

buttery_nipple.instructions: Pour the schnapps, then layer the cream liqueur on top over a bar spoon.
buttery_nipple.description: An American shot from the 1980s and a close relative of the Slippery Nipple: butterscotch schnapps and cream liqueur. It tastes like liquid toffee with cream. It is often served shaken rather than layered, which makes it even more dessert-like.

cable_car.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a glass rimmed with cinnamon sugar.
cable_car.description: Tony Abou-Ganim created the Cable Car in 1996 at the Starlight Room, a rooftop hotel bar past which San Francisco's famous cable cars run. It is a Sidecar made with spiced rum and a cinnamon-sugar rim.
cable_car.creator: Tony Abou-Ganim (Starlight Room)

cafe_brulot.instructions: Heat the cognac with the liqueur, spices, zest and sugar, flame it and douse with hot coffee.
cafe_brulot.description: Café brûlot ("burnt coffee") is a New Orleans tradition associated with Antoine's restaurant in the late 19th century. Spiced cognac is set alight in a silver bowl and then extinguished with hot coffee: a showy digestif with aromas of citrus and spice.
cafe_brulot.creator: Antoine's restaurant

cafe_royale.instructions: Place a sugar cube on a spoon over the coffee, pour cognac over it, light it and, once the sugar has melted, lower it into the coffee.
cafe_royale.description: Café Royale is a French tradition: cognac and a sugar cube are set alight on a spoon over a cup of coffee and, once the sugar caramelises, lowered into the drink. According to legend, it was a favourite of Napoleon.

caffe_corretto.instructions: Add liqueur or grappa to a freshly pulled espresso.
caffe_corretto.description: 'Corrected' coffee is an Italian espresso with a spoonful of grappa, sambuca or brandy. It is ordered in bars after lunch or, especially in the north of the country, in the morning. Sometimes the coffee is drunk first and the grappa poured into the still-warm cup.

caipirinha.instructions: Cut the lime into wedges and muddle with sugar right in the glass, add ice and cachaça, and stir.
caipirinha.description: Brazil's national cocktail, made with cachaça, a spirit distilled from fresh sugarcane juice. One version traces it to a folk remedy for the 1918 Spanish flu (cachaça, lime, honey and garlic), from which the garlic and honey eventually disappeared. The name is a diminutive of caipira, 'country dweller'. The lime is muddled right in the glass so the oils from the peel add aroma. Made with vodka instead of cachaça, it becomes a Caipiroska.

camerons_kick.description: A recipe from Harry MacElhone's 1922 book and The Savoy Cocktail Book: a sour built on two whiskies, Scotch and Irish, with almond orgeat. The nutty sweetness of the orgeat gently ties together the malty and peaty notes.

canchanchara.instructions: Dissolve the honey in the lime juice and water, add rum and ice, and stir.
canchanchara.description: Considered one of the oldest Cuban drinks, it was drunk by the Mambí rebels during the wars of independence in the second half of the 19th century, who mixed aguardiente with honey, lime and water. Today the Canchánchara is traditionally served in the town of Trinidad in small clay cups. It is the direct ancestor of the Daiquiri: simple, honeyed and refreshing.

canelazo.instructions: Simmer water with cinnamon and panela, add the juice and aguardiente, and serve hot.
canelazo.description: Canelazo is a hot drink from the high Andes of Ecuador, Colombia and Peru: cinnamon, cane sugar, fruit juice and aguardiente. It is drunk in the evenings in cold mountain cities such as Quito and Bogotá.

cantarito.instructions: Pour the tequila and juices into a chilled clay cup with ice and salt, and top up with soda.
cantarito.description: The Cantarito is a street drink from Jalisco, sold at roadside stands near the town of Tequila. The name comes from the small clay pot it is served in; the pot is soaked in water beforehand so it stays cold longer. A mix of three citrus juices, salt and soda makes it something like an expanded Paloma.

cape_codder.instructions: Build in a glass over ice and stir.
cape_codder.description: The cranberry growers' cooperative Ocean Spray promoted vodka with cranberry juice from the 1940s, first under the name Red Devil. The name Cape Codder refers to the Cape Cod peninsula, where cranberries are grown. This tart, berry highball is the base of a whole family: the Sea Breeze, Bay Breeze, Madras and Cosmopolitan.
cape_codder.creator: Ocean Spray

carajillo.instructions: Shake the liqueur and espresso with ice and strain over fresh ice (the Spanish version is hot coffee with brandy or rum).
carajillo.description: The Carajillo is a Spanish coffee drink with brandy or rum, which according to legend Spanish soldiers in Cuba drank for courage (coraje). In Mexico the cold version is popular: espresso shaken with ice and Licor 43, a vanilla-citrus liqueur. Today it is one of the most fashionable digestifs in Mexico City and in Spanish bars.

cardinale.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
cardinale.description: A popular story says the Cardinale appeared in Rome in the 1950s for a cardinal who wanted a drier Negroni. Dry vermouth and less Campari make it resemble a Dry Martini with a bitter edge. The deep red colour lives up to the name, like a cardinal's robes.

casa_blanca.description: A rum cocktail known from American drinks guides (it is in TheCocktailDB), with a touch of triple sec and maraschino. In essence it is a strong, dry Daiquiri with a cherry note.

casino.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
casino.description: Hugo Ensslin published the Casino in Recipes for Mixed Drinks (1916), the same book in which the Aviation first appeared. Essentially it is an Aviation without the crème de violette: gin, a little maraschino and lemon. The result is a dry, strong, aromatic cocktail that lets the gin shine through.
casino.creator: Hugo Ensslin

champagne_cocktail.instructions: Place a bitters-soaked sugar cube in a flute, add the cognac and slowly top up with Champagne.
champagne_cocktail.description: The Champagne Cocktail is one of the few drinks already in Jerry Thomas's 1862 book; the cognac came later. The Angostura-soaked sugar cube constantly releases bubbles, so the drink stays alive in the glass. In classic cinema it's ordered in Casablanca and other films; it's an elegant way to make a glass of Champagne more festive.

champs_elysees.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
champs_elysees.description: Named after Paris's grand avenue, the cocktail was published in the 1920s–30s, including in "The Savoy Cocktail Book". It is a cognac sour with Chartreuse — essentially a Sidecar where the orange liqueur gives way to an herbal one. Elegant, French in spirit and highly aromatic.

chancellor.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
chancellor.description: The Chancellor is Scotch with port and a dash of dry vermouth, known since the 1930s. Port brings berry sweetness and deep color, while the whisky's peaty notes give a warm finish. A good winter digestif.

chapman.instructions: Combine the sodas with grenadine over ice, add bitters and sliced fruit.
chapman.description: The Chapman is Nigeria's iconic 'non-alcoholic' drink, named, according to one version, after a bartender at a colonial-era Lagos club. Fanta, Sprite, grenadine and Angostura with cucumber — fruity, spicy and very refreshing. Strictly speaking, Angostura contains alcohol, but in such small amounts the drink is considered non-alcoholic.

charlie_chaplin.description: A cocktail from the bar of the old Waldorf-Astoria hotel, named after Charlie Chaplin. Equal parts sloe gin, apricot liqueur and lime: a tart, fruity and fairly low-proof drink.
charlie_chaplin.creator: Waldorf-Astoria bar

chartreuse_swizzle.instructions: Pour everything into a glass of crushed ice and swizzle with a swizzle stick until the glass frosts.
chartreuse_swizzle.description: Marco Dionysos created the Chartreuse Swizzle in the early 2000s in San Francisco, where it later became a signature at the renowned tiki bar Smuggler's Cove. Here the powerful, herbal green Chartreuse becomes the base of a tropical swizzle with falernum, pineapple and lime. The result is surprisingly refreshing and one of the most popular ways to drink Chartreuse.
chartreuse_swizzle.creator: Marco Dionysos

chatham_artillery_punch.instructions: Combine the spirits, juice and sugar in a bowl with a large block of ice; top up with Champagne just before serving.
chatham_artillery_punch.description: The famous punch of the Savannah, Georgia artillery regiment, known since the mid-19th century. Several spirits, lemon, sugar and Champagne: very strong, though it tastes light. There are many recipes; some include tea and red wine.
chatham_artillery_punch.creator: Chatham Artillery

chicago_fizz.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice, strain and top up with soda.
chicago_fizz.description: The Chicago Fizz is an early 20th-century fizz made with rum, port and egg white. The port tints the foam pink and adds berry depth; it appears in TheCocktailDB and old American bar books.

chilcano.instructions: Pour pisco and juice into an ice-filled glass, top up with ginger ale and add a dash of bitters.
chilcano.description: The Chilcano is Peru's most popular highball, essentially a Pisco Buck with ginger ale. It's linked to Italian immigrants in Peru, who made a similar drink with grappa. By one account, the name comes from chilcano, a Peruvian fish soup also known as a "reviving" dish. Light, refreshing and floral.

chimayo.description: The signature drink of Rancho de Chimayó restaurant in New Mexico, created in 1965 by Arturo Jaramillo. Local apple cider, tequila, crème de cassis and lemon: an autumnal, fruity and very regional cocktail.
chimayo.creator: Arturo Jaramillo (Rancho de Chimayó)

chocolate_cake_shot.instructions: Shake the vodka and liqueur with ice and strain; drink and immediately bite into the sugared lemon.
chocolate_cake_shot.description: This shot is a flavor illusion: hazelnut liqueur with vanilla vodka, chased with sugared lemon, tastes like chocolate cake in the mouth, even though there is no chocolate in it.

chocolate_martini.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a glass with a chocolate rim.
chocolate_martini.description: The Chocolate Martini is a child of the 1990s '-tini' craze: vodka with chocolate liqueur, sometimes with cream or Baileys. It is a martini only in its glass; in reality it is dessert in a glass.

chrysanthemum.description: The Chrysanthemum is a low-ABV cocktail of dry vermouth with Bénédictine and a dash of absinthe, known from books of the 1910s–30s, including "The Savoy Cocktail Book". An herbal, honeyed and elegant aperitif.

chuhai.instructions: Fill a glass with ice, add the shochu and lemon, and top up with sparkling water.
chuhai.description: Chuhai (short for "shochu highball") is one of the most popular drinks in Japanese izakayas: shochu with soda and juice, most often lemon ("lemon sour"). It's also sold in cans at every konbini.

cinderella.instructions: Shake the juices and grenadine with ice, strain over ice and top up with soda.
cinderella.description: The Cinderella is a classic non-alcoholic fruit punch that has been served to designated drivers and kids for decades. Orange, pineapple, lemon and grenadine with soda: balanced and bright.

cinnamon_toast_crunch.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a shot glass rimmed with cinnamon sugar.
cinnamon_toast_crunch.description: The shot is named after the American cinnamon cereal: cinnamon whisky liqueur and horchata-flavored cream rum liqueur. Sweet, creamy and spiced. One of the most Instagrammable shots of the 2010s, a fixture on US college bar menus.

classic_lemonade.instructions: Combine the juice and syrup, top up with water (or soda) and serve over ice.
classic_lemonade.description: Lemonade has been known since the 17th century: in 1670s Paris there was even a guild of lemonade sellers. Lemon juice, sugar and water form the base of countless cocktails and soft drinks; made with sparkling water, it becomes sparkling lemonade.

clerico.instructions: Combine the wine with the fruit and sugar, let it infuse in the fridge and serve over ice.
clerico.description: Clericó is South America's white-wine answer to sangria, a must on the New Year's table in Argentina and Uruguay (where the holiday falls in summer). The name probably comes from the British "claret cup".

clover_club.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice; strain into a chilled glass.
clover_club.description: Named after the Clover Club, a society of Philadelphia journalists and lawyers that met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel from the 1880s. It was popular before Prohibition, then all but forgotten, and returned in the 2000s — Julie Reiner's Brooklyn bar is even named after it. Raspberry and egg white give a soft pink, foamy texture, while the gin keeps the drink from turning cloying.

cobras_fang.instructions: Flash-blend with crushed ice and pour into a glass.
cobras_fang.description: Another early tiki drink by Donn Beach (1930s). Strong Demerara rum, passion fruit, falernum and citrus make a rich drink with a bite worthy of its name. The recipe was recovered by Jeff Berry from the notes of Donn's bartenders.
cobras_fang.creator: Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber)

coffee_cocktail.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain.
coffee_cocktail.description: A curiosity of cocktail history: Jerry Thomas's Coffee Cocktail (1887) contains neither coffee nor bitters. It is named for its colour and foam, which look like coffee with milk. Port, cognac and egg make a creamy dessert flip.
coffee_cocktail.creator: Jerry Thomas

cola_de_mono.instructions: Simmer milk with coffee, sugar and spices, let cool, add the spirit and serve cold.
cola_de_mono.description: Cola de Mono ("monkey's tail") is a Chilean Christmas drink of aguardiente, milk, coffee and spices, served cold. The origin of the name is disputed; one legend links it to President Pedro Montt and his Colt revolver ("Colt de Montt").

conference.instructions: Stir with ice and strain over a large cube.
conference.description: Brian Miller of Death & Co built an Old Fashioned on four spirits — two whiskeys, calvados and cognac — like a 'conference' of brown spirits. Complex, woody-fruity and dense.
conference.creator: Brian Miller (Death & Co)

coquito.instructions: Blend all ingredients, chill in a bottle and serve cold.
coquito.description: Coquito ('little coconut') is Puerto Rico's Christmas drink, a coconut cousin of eggnog, only without eggs. It is made in big batches, bottled and given to friends over the holidays. Creamy, sweet and spiced.

corn_n_oil.instructions: Pour the falernum, juice and rum over ice, stir and add Angostura on top.
corn_n_oil.description: Corn 'n' Oil is an old Barbadian drink of rum and falernum, a local spiced syrup (or liqueur) with lime, clove and almond. The name is explained in various ways: either the dark rum over the falernum looks like crude oil over corn oil, or it is a nod to the biblical "corn and oil". Today it is made with black blackstrap rum.

corpse_reviver_1.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
corpse_reviver_1.description: The first version of the Corpse Reviver from Harry Craddock's The Savoy Cocktail Book, meant for the morning or "when steam and energy are needed". Unlike the citrusy No. 2, this is a spirit-forward stirred drink: cognac, calvados and sweet vermouth. Warm, fruity and woody, it is closer to a brandy Manhattan.
corpse_reviver_1.creator: Harry Craddock

corpse_reviver_2.instructions: Rinse the glass with absinthe or add a dash to the shaker; shake with ice and strain.
corpse_reviver_2.description: Corpse Revivers are a family of 19th-century morning drinks meant to bring you back to life after a rough night. No. 2, from Harry Craddock's The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), became the most popular; Craddock wryly warned that four in quick succession would "unrevive the corpse again". Equal parts gin, Lillet, Cointreau and lemon with a drop of absinthe make it bright, dry and invigorating.
corpse_reviver_2.creator: Harry Craddock

cosmonaut.instructions: Shake with ice (the jam will dissolve) and double strain.
cosmonaut.description: Sasha Petraske created the Cosmonaut for Milk & Honey: a gin sour sweetened not with syrup but with a spoonful of raspberry jam. It is a simple recipe that is easy to make at home, and the jam gives rich berry flavour and texture.
cosmonaut.creator: Sasha Petraske

cosmopolitan.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
cosmopolitan.description: Similar recipes appeared in the 1970s–80s (Cheryl Cook of Miami Beach is often named), but the canonical version with citrus vodka, Cointreau, fresh lime and cranberry was popularized by Toby Cecchini at New York's Odeon in 1988. In the 1990s the TV series Sex and the City made it iconic. It is essentially a pink vodka Margarita — tart, berry-bright and instantly recognizable.
cosmopolitan.creator: Toby Cecchini (Odeon), popularizer

crodino_spritz.instructions: Pour the aperitif over ice, top up with soda and garnish with orange.
crodino_spritz.description: Italian non-alcoholic bitters such as Crodino (launched in 1965) and Sanbittèr make a ready-made base for an alcohol-free spritz. The bittersweet orange flavour and bubbles make it a proper aperitif without the alcohol.

cuba_libre.instructions: Pour the rum and lime juice into a glass with ice and top up with cola.
cuba_libre.description: The name "Free Cuba" was a slogan of the war of independence, and according to the popular story the cocktail appeared around 1900, when Coca-Cola arrived in Havana along with American soldiers. Rum, cola and lime make it one of the best-selling cocktails in the world. The lime matters: it's what sets a Cuba Libre apart from a plain rum and coke.

cucumber_cooler.instructions: Muddle the cucumber and mint with the juice and syrup, shake with ice, strain over ice and top up with soda.
cucumber_cooler.description: The Cucumber Cooler is a modern alcohol-free "spa drink": cucumber, mint, lime and soda. Very cooling and light, it is close in spirit to an alcohol-free Eastside.

daiquiri.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
daiquiri.description: As the popular story goes, the Daiquiri was invented around 1898 by American mining engineer Jennings Cox at the mines near the Cuban village of Daiquirí — though Cubans were drinking rum with lime and sugar long before that. The drink was made famous by El Floridita bar in Havana and its regular, Hemingway. A classic Daiquiri is not a frozen dessert but a lean, balanced sour that bartenders use to test each other: if the Daiquiri is good, you can trust the bar.
daiquiri.creator: Jennings Cox (according to legend)

daisy_de_santiago.instructions: Shake rum, lime and syrup, pour over crushed ice, top up with soda and float the Chartreuse on top.
daisy_de_santiago.description: Described by Charles Baker in The Gentleman's Companion (1939), who tried it in Santiago, Cuba. A Daiquiri over crushed ice with a float of yellow Chartreuse: honeyed, herbal and very fresh.

dark_n_stormy.instructions: Pour the ginger beer over ice, then carefully float the rum on top.
dark_n_stormy.description: Bermuda's national drink: the Gosling family's dark rum and spicy ginger beer brewed at the local British naval base. According to legend, the name came from a sailor who said the drink looked like "a cloud you wouldn't want to meet at sea". Gosling's trademarked the Dark 'n Stormy, so "officially" it can only be made with their rum.
dark_n_stormy.creator: The Gosling family

de_la_louisiane.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
de_la_louisiane.description: The signature cocktail of New Orleans' Restaurant de la Louisiane, published in 1937. It is a sweet, rich relative of the Vieux Carré: rye, vermouth and Bénédictine combined with absinthe and Peychaud's bitters.
de_la_louisiane.creator: Restaurant de la Louisiane

death_flip.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain; dust with nutmeg.
death_flip.description: Chris Hysted-Adams created the Death Flip in Melbourne around 2010, combining seemingly incompatible ingredients: tequila, Chartreuse and Jägermeister with a whole egg. The result is a velvety, herbal-spiced flip that became one of Australia's best-known cocktails.
death_flip.creator: Chris Hysted-Adams

death_in_the_afternoon.instructions: Pour absinthe into a glass and slowly top up with chilled Champagne until the drink turns cloudy.
death_in_the_afternoon.description: Ernest Hemingway contributed this recipe to the celebrity collection So Red the Nose (1935), naming it after his book on bullfighting. He advised pouring Champagne into absinthe "until it attains the proper opalescent milkiness" and drinking three to five of them slowly. Anise-laden absinthe and dry Champagne make an unusual, sharp and invigorating combination.
death_in_the_afternoon.creator: Ernest Hemingway

diabolo_menthe.instructions: Pour the syrup into a glass and top up with cold lemonade.
diabolo_menthe.description: The Diabolo is a French café classic: lemonade with fruit syrup, the best-known version being bright green with mint. Schoolchildren and adults order it in cafés all over France; there are also versions with grenadine (diabolo grenadine) and strawberry.

diesel.instructions: Mix beer and cola in equal parts.
diesel.description: In Germany, a Diesel (also Colabier or Krefelder) is beer mixed half and half with cola; in Britain the word sometimes refers to a mix of lager, cider and blackcurrant cordial. A sweet, fizzy, low-alcohol drink for a hot day.

diki_diki.description: A cocktail from The Savoy Cocktail Book: calvados, Swedish punsch (an arrack-based liqueur) and grapefruit. Craddock dedicated it to the chief of a Philippine tribe; spicy, appley and slightly bitter.

division_bell.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
division_bell.description: Phil Ward created the Division Bell for the opening of his agave bar Mayahuel in 2009; the name references the Pink Floyd album. It's another descendant of the Last Word: smoky mezcal, bittersweet Aperol, maraschino and lime. Its bright orange color and pairing of smoke with citrus made it a modern classic.
division_bell.creator: Phil Ward (Mayahuel)

doctor_funk.instructions: Shake rum, lime, grenadine and absinthe, pour over crushed ice and top up with soda.
doctor_funk.description: The drink is named after Bernard Funk, a German doctor who lived in Samoa in the late 19th century and, according to legend, treated patients with this cocktail; Robert Louis Stevenson was one of them. Donn Beach later adapted the recipe for tiki bars.

dry_martini.instructions: Stir with ice until well chilled and strain into a chilled glass.
dry_martini.description: The Dry Martini evolved from the sweeter Martinez: by the early 20th century the vermouth had turned dry and its share kept shrinking. The ratio is an eternal argument, from 2:1 in early recipes to almost neat gin by mid-century. The drink became a symbol of American cocktail culture, and both Churchill and Roosevelt drank it. An olive garnish adds a briny note, a lemon twist a fresher aroma; the version with olive brine is called the Dirty Martini.

dubonnet_cocktail.instructions: Stir with ice and strain (or serve on the rocks).
dubonnet_cocktail.description: Dubonnet is a French aromatised wine aperitif with quinine. Mixed with gin it is called a Zaza; in Britain it was the favourite aperitif of the Queen Mother and later of Queen Elizabeth II. Fruity, slightly bitter and elegant.

duck_fart.instructions: Layer: coffee liqueur, cream liqueur, whisky.
duck_fart.description: A jokingly named shot from Anchorage, Alaska: coffee liqueur, cream liqueur and Canadian whisky in layers. It resembles a B-52, but with whisky instead of orange liqueur.

earl_grey_marteani.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain into a sugar-rimmed glass.
earl_grey_marteani.description: Audrey Saunders created the Earl Grey MarTEAni in the early 2000s, infusing gin with bergamot tea. The tea's floral, citrusy aroma sits beautifully in a gin sour with egg white. The drink was one of the first popular examples of infusions in modern bars.
earl_grey_marteani.creator: Audrey Saunders

eastside.instructions: Muddle the cucumber, add the rest, shake with ice and double strain.
eastside.description: The Eastside is a Southside with cucumber, credited to George Delgado of New York's Libation (mid-2000s). Cucumber and mint make the gin sour even cooler and "greener"; it is one of the best summer cocktails.
eastside.creator: George Delgado

egg_cream.instructions: Pour in the syrup and milk, then add seltzer in a strong stream, stirring vigorously with a spoon until foamy.
egg_cream.description: A New York soda-fountain classic: despite the name, an egg cream contains neither eggs nor cream. Chocolate syrup, milk and seltzer, stirred vigorously, make a foamy, light milk drink.

eggnog.instructions: Dry shake all ingredients, then shake with ice and strain; dust with nutmeg. For a crowd, make a large batch in a punch bowl.
eggnog.description: Eggnog descends from the medieval British posset, hot milk with ale or wine, and in the 18th-century American colonies rum turned it into an affordable festive drink. According to legend, George Washington served guests his own potent recipe. Today it is the quintessential Christmas drink in the US and Canada: creamy and spiced.

eierpunsch.instructions: Whisk the yolks with sugar and vanilla over a water bath, gradually adding warm wine, until thick and foamy.
eierpunsch.description: Eierpunsch is a hot egg-and-wine punch from German Christmas markets, close to Italian zabaglione. Thick, sweet and frothy; often served with cream and sometimes a splash of rum.

el_capitan.description: El Capitán is a Peruvian "pisco Manhattan", invented according to legend by army captains in the Andes who warmed themselves with a mix of pisco and vermouth. Floral pisco with vermouth makes a light, aromatic stirred cocktail.

el_diablo.instructions: Shake the tequila, cassis and lime with ice, strain into an ice-filled glass and top up with ginger beer.
el_diablo.description: The recipe was first published in Trader Vic's 1946 book under the name Mexican El Diablo. Tequila was still exotic in the US at the time, and Vic paired it with ginger and blackcurrant. The result is a deep ruby, spicy, berry-driven long drink, similar to a Moscow Mule but more complex.
el_diablo.creator: Trader Vic

el_presidente.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
el_presidente.description: An elegant rum cocktail from the Prohibition era, when Americans traveled to Havana to drink. It is named after one of Cuba's presidents of the 1910s–20s (Mario Menocal or Gerardo Machado are usually cited). It is a rarity as a stirred rum drink: mellow vermouth, orange liqueur and a touch of grenadine make it something like a rum Manhattan — fruity and silky.

electric_lemonade.instructions: Shake the vodka, liqueur, juice and syrup, strain over ice and top up with lemonade.
electric_lemonade.description: Electric Lemonade is a bright blue party cocktail: vodka, blue curaçao, lemon and soda. A relative of the Blue Lagoon but with fresh lemon juice; sweet, tart and very eye-catching in the glass.

english_rose.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a sugar-rimmed glass.
english_rose.description: The English Rose is a 1930s cocktail of gin, dry vermouth and apricot liqueur, tinted with grenadine. Served with a sugar rim, it's fruity but not cloying, thanks to the vermouth.

enzoni.instructions: Muddle the grapes with the syrup, add the rest, shake with ice and strain over ice.
enzoni.description: Vincenzo Errico created the Enzoni at Milk & Honey, turning the Negroni into a refreshing sour. Muddled grapes bring juicy sweetness, lemon adds freshness and Campari its signature bitterness.
enzoni.creator: Vincenzo Errico (Milk & Honey)

erdbeerbowle.instructions: Sprinkle the strawberries with sugar, cover with wine and leave to infuse for a couple of hours; top up with sparkling wine before serving.
erdbeerbowle.description: Bowle is a German summer punch of wine, sparkling wine and fruit; the strawberry version is the most popular. It is made in a large glass bowl for garden parties. Mellow, berry-forward and light.

espresso_martini.instructions: Shake hard with ice and double strain into a chilled glass for a thick crema.
espresso_martini.description: According to legend, Dick Bradsell came up with the cocktail in the 1980s for a model who asked for "something to wake me up and then mess me up" (the original phrase was cruder). The drink was first called the Vodka Espresso, later the Pharmaceutical Stimulant, and in a martini glass it became the Espresso Martini. In the 2020s it enjoyed a new wave of popularity and once again became one of the most-ordered cocktails in the world. The keys are fresh espresso and a hard shake for a creamy foam.
espresso_martini.creator: Dick Bradsell

espresso_tonic.instructions: Pour tonic over ice and slowly pour the espresso over the top.
espresso_tonic.description: The Espresso Tonic, according to one version, was invented at the Swedish coffee shop Koppi in 2007 and quickly spread through third-wave coffee shops. Bitter tonic with bright, acidic espresso makes a refreshing summer coffee drink that separates beautifully into layers.
espresso_tonic.creator: Koppi coffee shop (according to one version)

fancy_free.instructions: Stir with ice and strain over ice.
fancy_free.description: The Fancy Free is a 1940s Old Fashioned in which the sugar is replaced with maraschino cherry liqueur. This gives the drink a floral, almond aroma and makes it a touch drier. A simple, elegant option for bourbon lovers.

fernandito.instructions: Pour the Fernet over ice and slowly top up with cola (the foam rises fast).
fernandito.description: In Argentina, especially in Córdoba, 'fernet con coca' is practically the national drink: the country consumes most of the world's Fernet-Branca. The Italian bitter was brought over by immigrants, and its pairing with cola took off in the second half of the 20th century. Bitter, herbal, minty and sweet all at once — a taste that shocks at first and then hooks you.

feuerzangenbowle.instructions: Fix a sugarloaf over a bowl of hot spiced wine, soak it with rum and set it alight until the sugar drips into the wine as caramel.
feuerzangenbowle.description: "Fire-tongs punch" is a German tradition: a sugarloaf is set over a bowl of mulled wine, soaked with rum and set alight, and the caramel drips into the wine. It owes much of its popularity to the film "Die Feuerzangenbowle" (1944), which students watch at Christmas.

final_ward.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
final_ward.description: Phil Ward created the Final Ward at Death & Co, swapping the gin in the Last Word for rye and the lime for lemon. The name is a play on the creator's surname and the original. Spicy rye makes the drink richer and warmer while keeping Chartreuse's herbal power. A great choice for those who find the Last Word too light.
final_ward.creator: Phil Ward (Death & Co)

fish_house_punch.instructions: Mix in a punch bowl with a large block of ice (usually as a batch for a group) and ladle out.
fish_house_punch.description: The punch of the Schuylkill Fishing Company, a fishing club founded in Philadelphia in 1732, and one of the oldest American recipes. Rum, cognac and peach brandy with lemon, sugar and water. Legend has it that after drinking it George Washington could not write in his diary for three days.
fish_house_punch.creator: Schuylkill Fishing Company club

fitzgerald.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over ice or into a chilled glass.
fitzgerald.description: Dale DeGroff, one of the fathers of the cocktail revival, created the Fitzgerald in the 1990s at the Rainbow Room. It's a gin sour with a couple of dashes of Angostura that add spicy depth. A strikingly simple recipe that shows how bitters can transform a drink.
fitzgerald.creator: Dale DeGroff

flaming_dr_pepper.instructions: Light the amaretto and rum shot, drop it into a glass of beer (the flame goes out) and drink in one go.
flaming_dr_pepper.description: A shot that supposedly tastes like Dr Pepper soda, though it contains none: amaretto with a float of overproof rum is set alight and dropped into beer. The fire makes it dangerous, so it should only be made by experienced bartenders.

flaming_lamborghini.instructions: Pour coffee liqueur and sambuca into a glass and ignite; drink it flaming through a straw while topping up with curaçao and Baileys from shot glasses.
flaming_lamborghini.description: The Flaming Lamborghini is a showpiece shot: a burning mix of sambuca and coffee liqueur drunk through a straw while the bartender pours in curaçao and cream liqueur. Spectacular but dangerous, so handle with care.

flirtini.instructions: Shake the vodka, liqueur and juice, strain and top up with champagne.
flirtini.description: The Flirtini is a Sex and the City-era cocktail that became popular in the early 2000s. Pineapple, orange liqueur, vodka and champagne make a light, festive drink made for a hen party.

floradora.instructions: Shake the gin, lime and syrup with ice, strain into an ice-filled glass and top up with ginger ale.
floradora.description: The cocktail is named after the Broadway musical Florodora (1900), famous for its sextet of chorus girls. Legend has it that it was created at the Imperial Hotel bar at the request of one of the "Florodora girls". A pink, berry-and-ginger long drink that came back into fashion in the 2000s.

florida_mocktail.instructions: Shake the juices and syrup with ice, strain over ice and top up with soda.
florida_mocktail.description: The Florida is a Prohibition-era non-alcoholic cocktail named after the citrus state: grapefruit, orange and lemon with soda. Dry, slightly bitter and very refreshing, it's a worthy grown-up mocktail.

fog_cutter.instructions: Shake everything except the sherry with ice, pour over crushed ice and float the sherry on top.
fog_cutter.description: Trader Vic joked about his Fog Cutter: "After two of these, you won't even see the stuff." Three spirits (rum, brandy and gin) plus orange, lemon, orgeat and a sherry float. It's one of the major tiki classics, known for its strength and complex nutty aroma.
fog_cutter.creator: Trader Vic

ford_cocktail.description: George Kappeler's 1895 recipe: a 50/50 martini made with Old Tom gin and a spoonful of Bénédictine. The liqueur's honeyed, herbal touch makes it softer and more aromatic than the classic martini of the era.
ford_cocktail.creator: George Kappeler

french_75.instructions: Shake the gin, juice and syrup with ice, strain into a flute and top up with champagne.
french_75.description: The drink is named after the French 75mm field gun of World War I; it was said to hit with the same force. Early versions appeared in Paris around 1915 (Harry's New York Bar is often cited), and the gin-and-champagne recipe was fixed in The Savoy Cocktail Book. In New Orleans a cognac version is popular. In essence it is a Tom Collins with champagne in place of soda.
french_75.creator: Harry MacElhone (one version)

french_connection.instructions: Build in an ice-filled glass and stir.
french_connection.description: The cognac sibling of the Godfather, named after the film The French Connection (1971) starring Gene Hackman. Cognac and amaretto make a simple after-dinner pairing: the spirit's fruity, woody character is softened by the liqueur's almond sweetness. The proportions are often tilted toward the cognac.

french_martini.instructions: Shake hard with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
french_martini.description: The French Martini appeared in the late 1980s at restaurateur Keith McNally's New York venues and became one of the symbols of the "-tini" era of sweet drinks served in a martini glass. It is called French because of the Chambord raspberry liqueur. Pineapple juice gives it a pleasant velvety foam when shaken.
french_martini.creator: Keith McNally's bars

frisco_sour.description: A sour in which the sugar is replaced by honeyed, herbal Bénédictine and the citrus by a mix of lemon and lime. The name refers to San Francisco; the recipe appears in mid-20th-century American bar guides and in TheCocktailDB.

fuzzy_navel.instructions: Pour into a glass with ice and stir.
fuzzy_navel.description: The Fuzzy Navel appeared in the 1980s, when DeKuyper Peachtree schnapps became a best-seller in the US. "Fuzzy" comes from the peach's velvety skin, "navel" from the navel orange. A very sweet, simple highball; with vodka it's called a Hairy Navel, and with Champagne a Fuzzy Navel Royale.

galliano_hot_shot.instructions: Pour the Galliano, then hot coffee on top, then a layer of cream.
galliano_hot_shot.description: A warm shot popular in Sweden since the 1980s: cold vanilla Galliano, hot coffee and a layer of cream. A contrast of temperatures and flavours, like a mini Irish Coffee.

garibaldi.instructions: Pour Campari over ice and top up with whipped (aerated) orange juice.
garibaldi.description: Named after Giuseppe Garibaldi, the unifier of Italy: Campari from Milan and oranges from Sicily stand for the north and south of the country. The modern craze for it was started by New York's Dante, where the juice is whipped in a high-speed juicer to a 'fluffy' texture. A simple, bittersweet, juicy and low-proof aperitivo.

gimlet.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass. Classically, gin and lime cordial in a 2:1 ratio.
gimlet.description: The Gimlet is linked to the British Navy: from 1867 sailors were required to receive lime juice against scurvy, and Lauchlan Rose's preserved cordial mixed beautifully with gin. The name is credited either to naval surgeon Thomas Gimlette or to the gimlet, the tool used to tap barrels. In The Long Goodbye, Raymond Chandler insisted that a real Gimlet is nothing but gin and Rose's. Modern bartenders often make it with fresh lime or a house cordial.

gin_and_it.instructions: Stir with ice and strain (historically served at room temperature, without ice).
gin_and_it.description: 'It' is short for Italian, meaning Italian sweet vermouth. Gin and It was drunk in British pubs of the early 20th century, often at room temperature. It is a stripped-down Martinez without maraschino or bitters — sweet, herbal and simple.

gin_and_juice.instructions: Pour into an ice-filled glass and stir.
gin_and_juice.description: This most basic highball of gin and citrus juice became famous thanks to Snoop Dogg's song "Gin and Juice" (1994). There is no strict recipe: most often it is orange juice, grapefruit juice or a mix. Refreshing and very easy to make.

gin_and_tonic.instructions: Fill a glass with ice, add gin, top up with tonic and stir gently.
gin_and_tonic.description: The Gin & Tonic was born in British colonial India: the quinine in tonic protected against malaria, while gin, sugar and lime made the bitter medicine more palatable. Churchill said the gin and tonic had saved more Englishmen's lives than all the doctors in the Empire. In the 2010s, the Spanish craze for the "gintonic" in balloon glasses with botanical garnishes made it a bar hit once again.

gin_basil_smash.instructions: Muddle the basil with the lemon juice in a shaker, add the rest and ice, shake and double strain over fresh ice.
gin_basil_smash.description: Jörg Meyer created this cocktail in 2008 at Le Lion in Hamburg, originally calling it the Gin Pesto. Bright green, aromatic and simple, it became one of the most recognizable cocktails of the new century and a bestseller in bars worldwide. The secret is a generous handful of fresh basil, thoroughly muddled in the shaker.
gin_basil_smash.creator: Jörg Meyer (Le Lion)

gin_daisy.instructions: Shake with ice, strain over crushed ice and top up with soda.
gin_daisy.description: The Gin Daisy is one of the most popular daisies of the early 20th century. In the American version, the liqueur gave way to grenadine, making the drink pink and fruity; over crushed ice with soda it's especially refreshing.

gin_fizz.instructions: Shake the gin, juice and syrup with ice, strain into the glass and top up with soda.
gin_fizz.description: Fizzes are a family of refreshing sparkling drinks that became popular in America in the late 19th century; the Gin Fizz was first described in the 1876 edition of Jerry Thomas's book. Unlike a Collins, a fizz is shaken and served in a smaller glass, usually without ice. Variations include the Silver Fizz with egg white, the Golden Fizz with yolk and the Royal Fizz with a whole egg.

gin_gin_mule.instructions: Muddle mint with the syrup and juice, add gin and ice, shake, strain into an ice-filled glass and top up with ginger beer.
gin_gin_mule.description: Audrey Saunders created the Gin-Gin Mule around 2000, before she opened her Pegu Club. It's a gin hybrid of the Mojito and the Moscow Mule: mint, lime and spicy ginger beer. It was one of the first "modern classics" of the New York cocktail renaissance and still works beautifully as a summer long drink.
gin_gin_mule.creator: Audrey Saunders

gin_rickey.instructions: Squeeze the lime into an ice-filled glass, drop the spent half in, add the gin and top up with soda.
gin_rickey.description: The Rickey was created in the 1880s at Shoomaker's bar in Washington for lobbyist Colonel Joe Rickey, who drank bourbon with lime and soda. Later the Rickey came to be made mostly with gin. Unlike a Collins, it has no sugar: the drink is dry, tart and very refreshing. The Rickey is Washington's official cocktail.
gin_rickey.creator: Colonel Joe Rickey, George Williamson (Shoomaker's bar)

gin_sling.instructions: Build in an ice-filled glass and dust with nutmeg.
gin_sling.description: Slings are one of the oldest families of mixed drinks: spirit, sugar and water with spice (often nutmeg). The Gin Sling has been known since the early 19th century, and this is the formula the famous Singapore Sling grew out of.

gin_swizzle.instructions: Swizzle in the glass with crushed ice using a swizzle stick and top up with soda.
gin_swizzle.description: The Gin Swizzle is one of the oldest versions of the Caribbean swizzle, popular in the British colonies. Lime, sugar and Angostura swizzled with crushed ice until the glass frosts make it ice-cold and refreshing.

godfather.instructions: Pour into a glass with ice and stir.
godfather.description: A cocktail named after Coppola's 1972 film The Godfather, although the pairing of whisky and amaretto was hardly "invented" by anyone. The almond-apricot sweetness of amaretto softens the Scotch, making this a very approachable digestif. It has relatives: the vodka-based Godmother and the Godchild, made with cream.

gold_rush.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over a large ice cube.
gold_rush.description: The Gold Rush was created in the early 2000s at Sasha Petraske's Milk & Honey in New York, one of the hubs of the cocktail renaissance. It is simply a Whiskey Sour with honey syrup instead of sugar, but honey and bourbon make a remarkably harmonious pair. It became one of the first modern classics and the direct ancestor of the Penicillin.
gold_rush.creator: T.J. Siegal (Milk & Honey)

golden_cadillac.description: The drink hails from Poor Red's in El Dorado, California, where according to legend it was created in 1952 for a newlywed couple who arrived in a gold Cadillac. At one time this small bar was the largest buyer of Galliano in the US. A creamy vanilla-chocolate dessert.
golden_cadillac.creator: Poor Red's Bar-B-Q

golden_dream.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
golden_dream.description: The Golden Dream is credited to Raimundo Alvarez of the Old King Cole Lounge in Hialeah, Florida, who reportedly made it for Joan Crawford around 1960. Vanilla-anise Galliano, orange and cream give it a dessert-like flavor reminiscent of an orange creamsicle. A typical example of the mid-century "cream" cocktails.
golden_dream.creator: Raimundo Alvarez (Old King Cole Lounge)

goombay_smash.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over ice.
goombay_smash.description: The Goombay Smash is the signature drink of the Blue Bee Bar on Green Turtle Cay in the Bahamas, where the owner, Miss Emily Cummins, kept the recipe secret. The name comes from goombay, traditional Bahamian music. A sweet tropical punch made with coconut rum.
goombay_smash.creator: Miss Emily (Blue Bee Bar)

grasshopper.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
