grasshopper.description: New Orleans restaurant Tujague's claims its owner Philibert Guichet invented the Grasshopper in 1918 for a competition in New York. It peaked in the 1950s and '60s, especially in the American Midwest, where a "grown-up" ice cream version was common. It's a pale green dessert in a glass that tastes like mint chocolate.
grasshopper.creator: Philibert Guichet (Tujague's)

green_mexican.instructions: Pour the green banana liqueur, layer the tequila on top and add a drop of lime.
green_mexican.description: The Green Mexican is a shot of Pisang Ambon green banana liqueur and tequila, popular in the Netherlands, Germany and Russia. The sweet banana masks the tequila's bite, while the lime adds freshness.

green_tea_shot.instructions: Shake the whiskey, schnapps and mix with ice, strain into a shot glass and add a splash of soda.
green_tea_shot.description: Despite the name, there is no green tea in this shot — it just looks like it. Irish whiskey, peach schnapps and sweet-and-sour mix make it one of the most popular shots in American bars of the 2000s–2010s.

greenpoint.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
greenpoint.description: Another Brooklyn-neighbourhood Manhattan, from Michael McIlroy of Milk & Honey (2006). Yellow Chartreuse brings a honeyed, herbal sweetness, making the drink softer and more aromatic than the original.
greenpoint.creator: Michael McIlroy (Milk & Honey)

greyhound.instructions: Pour into an ice-filled glass and stir.
greyhound.description: A similar mix of gin and grapefruit appears in Harry Craddock's book (1930), but the name Greyhound, according to one version, first appeared in 1945 on the menu of the Greyhound bus company's station restaurants. Later, vodka increasingly replaced the gin. It is a bittersweet, tart and refreshing drink, and with a salt rim it becomes a Salty Dog.

grog.instructions: Dissolve honey in hot water, add rum and lemon juice, and garnish with spices.
grog.description: In 1740, Admiral Edward Vernon ordered that sailors' daily rum ration be diluted with water to curb drunkenness. The admiral was nicknamed Old Grog after his coat of coarse grogram cloth, and the drink became "grog". Lemon juice against scurvy and sugar were added later; in modern Europe, grog means hot rum with water, honey and spices.
grog.creator: Admiral Edward Vernon

gummy_bear_shot.instructions: Shake the vodka and schnapps with ice, strain into a shot glass and top up with soda.
gummy_bear_shot.description: A shot that tastes like gummy bears: raspberry vodka, peach schnapps and a splash of soda. Very sweet and candy-like, often garnished with a real gummy bear.

halekulani.description: A 1930s cocktail from the Halekulani hotel in Honolulu, revived by Jeff Berry. Bourbon with three juices, grenadine and bitters: tropical, but with a warm whiskey base.
halekulani.creator: Halekulani Hotel

hanky_panky.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
hanky_panky.description: Ada "Coley" Coleman was the first famous female bartender and head of the American Bar at the Savoy before Harry Craddock. She created this drink for the actor Charles Hawtrey, who asked for something with a bit of punch; after tasting it he exclaimed, "That is the real hanky-panky!" A little Fernet-Branca turns a simple mix of gin and vermouth into a rich, bitter-herbal drink.
hanky_panky.creator: Ada Coleman (American Bar, Savoy)

harvard.instructions: Stir with ice, strain and add a splash of soda.
harvard.description: The Harvard is a cognac Manhattan known since the 1890s, with a splash of soda for lightness. Its traditional rival is the gin-based Yale Cocktail. Smooth, aromatic and somewhat collegiate in origin.

harvey_wallbanger.instructions: Pour the vodka and juice into an ice-filled glass, stir, and carefully float the Galliano on top.
harvey_wallbanger.description: The Harvey Wallbanger is a Screwdriver with a float of vanilla-anise Galliano. Popular legend tells of a surfer named Harvey who banged into walls after a few drinks, but the cocktail became hugely popular in the 1970s thanks to a Galliano ad campaign featuring a cartoon character. It is a symbol of disco-era American bar culture.

havana_cocktail.description: A simple rum cocktail with pineapple and a dash of lemon, known from mid-century American guides (it is in TheCocktailDB). The pineapple foams up when shaken, and the lemon keeps the sweetness in check. A good base for experimenting.

hemingway_special.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
hemingway_special.description: Constantino Ribalaigua, the legendary bartender at Havana's El Floridita, made this version of the Daiquiri for Ernest Hemingway. The writer reportedly had diabetes and wanted no sugar, but loved double measures of rum — hence the drink's other name, Papa Doble. Grapefruit and maraschino make it drier and more complex than a regular Daiquiri, though modern versions still leave room for some sugar for balance.
hemingway_special.creator: Constantino Ribalaigua (El Floridita)

hiroshima.instructions: Pour sambuca, layer cream liqueur over a bar spoon, then absinthe; drop grenadine on top so it sinks through the layers like a cloud.
hiroshima.description: The Hiroshima is a layered shot popular in bars in Russia and Eastern Europe: sambuca, cream liqueur, absinthe and a drop of grenadine that slowly sinks through the layers, resembling an explosion. Strong and very anise-forward.

horses_neck.instructions: Place a lemon peel spiral in the glass, hanging it over the rim, fill with ice, add the cognac and top up with ginger ale.
horses_neck.description: In the 1890s the Horse's Neck was a non-alcoholic drink of ginger ale and lemon; cognac or bourbon was added later — 'with a kick', as they said back then. The name comes from the long peel spiral hanging out of the glass like a horse's neck. The drink was popular in the Royal Navy.

hot_apple_cider.instructions: Heat the juice with the spices and zest without letting it boil, then strain.
hot_apple_cider.description: Hot spiced apple cider (in the American sense, unfiltered apple juice) is an autumn and winter drink of fairs and holidays. Cinnamon, cloves and zest make it resemble a non-alcoholic mulled wine; add rum or brandy for a grown-up version.

hot_buttered_rum.instructions: Mix the butter with sugar and spices in a mug, add rum and hot water, and stir.
hot_buttered_rum.description: Hot buttered rum was drunk in 18th-century colonial New England, when rum made from Caribbean molasses was America's main spirit. Butter, brown sugar and spices turn the rum into a warming drink close to a dessert. A 'batter' — a mix of butter, sugar and spices kept in the fridge — is usually made ahead.

hot_toddy.instructions: Dissolve the honey in hot water, add the whisky and lemon juice, and garnish with spices.
hot_toddy.description: The toddy has been known since the 18th century; the name probably came from India, where "toddy" meant fermented palm sap. In Britain and Ireland, hot whisky with honey, lemon and water became the classic folk remedy for colds. It's a warming, aromatic drink, and the spices can be varied to taste.
hot_toddy.garnish: lemon wheel studded with cloves, cinnamon stick

hotel_georgia.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain.
hotel_georgia.description: The 1940s signature cocktail of the Hotel Georgia in Vancouver. A gin sour with almond orgeat, egg white and orange flower water: delicate, floral, with a velvety foam.
hotel_georgia.creator: Hotel Georgia

hotel_nacional.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
hotel_nacional.description: The signature cocktail of Havana's Hotel Nacional de Cuba, which opened in 1930 and became a haven for American celebrities during Prohibition. It is credited either to bartender Wil Taylor or to Eddie Woelke. It is a Daiquiri with pineapple and apricot — fruity, yet still fresh.

hugo.instructions: Gently muddle the mint in the glass, add syrup, juice and ice, pour in prosecco and soda, and stir.
hugo.description: Bartender Roland Gruber created the Hugo in 2005 in South Tyrol as an alternative to the Aperol Spritz. The original recipe used lemon balm syrup, but it was soon replaced with elderflower syrup. The drink spread rapidly through Germany, Austria and the rest of Europe. It is a floral, minty and very light spritz.
hugo.creator: Roland Gruber

hurricane.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into an ice-filled glass.
hurricane.description: The Hurricane appeared in the 1940s at Pat O'Brien's bar in New Orleans; according to legend, the owner had to offload unpopular rum that distributors forced on him alongside whiskey. It was served in glasses shaped like hurricane lamps, which is how the glass itself got its name. Today it is the signature drink of Mardi Gras, although tourist bars often make it from a sweet premixed base.
hurricane.creator: Pat O'Brien's

ice_pick.instructions: Pour vodka into a glass over ice and top up with iced tea and lemon juice.
ice_pick.description: The Ice Pick is a simple highball of vodka and iced tea with lemon (listed in TheCocktailDB). It is essentially a 'real' spiked iced tea — unlike the Long Island, which contains no tea at all.

illegal.instructions: Shake with ice (if using egg white, dry shake first) and strain into a chilled glass.
illegal.description: The cocktail was created around 2011 by New York bartenders Lynnette Marrero and Jim Meehan for Ilegal mezcal. It combines smoky mezcal with overproof rum and spicy falernum — a hybrid of the Daiquiri and tiki culture. The name plays on both the brand and the "contraband" past of mezcal, which for a long time was smuggled across the border unofficially.
illegal.creator: Lynnette Marrero and Jim Meehan

improved_whiskey_cocktail.description: 'Improved' cocktails were a 19th-century step beyond the simple Old Fashioned: in 1876 Jerry Thomas added maraschino and absinthe to the formula. The result is an aromatic, complex Old Fashioned — effectively an ancestor of the Sazerac.
improved_whiskey_cocktail.creator: Jerry Thomas

ipanema.instructions: Muddle lime with sugar, add crushed ice and passion fruit juice, and top up with ginger ale.
ipanema.description: The Ipanema is an alcohol-free caipirinha named after Rio de Janeiro's famous beach: lime muddled with sugar, passion fruit and ginger ale. Refreshing, tart and tropical.

irish_coffee.instructions: Warm the glass, dissolve the sugar in hot coffee, add the whiskey and gently float the cream over a spoon. Do not stir.
irish_coffee.description: Chef Joe Sheridan created the drink in 1943 at the Foynes flying-boat terminal to warm up frozen transatlantic passengers; asked whether it was Brazilian coffee, he replied, "No, it's Irish." In 1952 journalist Stanton Delaplane brought the recipe to the Buena Vista in San Francisco, which still makes thousands a day. The key is to sip the hot coffee and whiskey through a layer of cool cream.
irish_coffee.creator: Joe Sheridan

irish_flag.description: A layered shot in the colours of the Irish flag: green, white and orange. Especially popular on St Patrick's Day. The order of the layers matters: the heavy crème de menthe goes at the bottom, the light orange liqueur on top.

irish_maid.instructions: Muddle the cucumber, add the rest, shake with ice and strain.
irish_maid.description: A member of the 'Maid' family of cucumber sours created by bartenders at New York's Milk & Honey/Little Branch and popularized by Sean Muldoon. Irish whiskey, elderflower and cucumber make a bright, floral and very fresh sour.
irish_maid.creator: Sean Muldoon (Dead Rabbit)

irish_slammer.instructions: Pour whiskey and cream liqueur into a shot glass, drop it into half a pint of stout and down it before the liqueur curdles.
irish_slammer.description: A "bomb" shot of Irish whiskey and cream liqueur dropped into stout. In the US it was long known by a name referencing the conflict in Northern Ireland, which many bars and the Irish themselves consider offensive, so today it's more often called the Irish Slammer.
irish_slammer.creator: Charles Oberg (by one account)

jack_rose.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
jack_rose.description: The Jack Rose is made with applejack, the American apple brandy (Laird's is the oldest licensed distillery in the US), and was hugely fashionable in the early 20th century. The name is usually explained as "jack" from applejack plus the rose color from grenadine, though there are also legends about a gangster named Jack Rose. Hemingway mentions it in The Sun Also Rises. Today it's often made with Calvados.

jagerbomb.instructions: Pour the energy drink into a glass and drop in a shot of Jägermeister; drink immediately.
jagerbomb.description: The Jägerbomb is a 2000s club classic: a shot of the German herbal liqueur Jägermeister dropped into a glass of energy drink. The name comes from the 'bomb' serve, where the shot is dropped into the glass. Combining alcohol with lots of caffeine masks intoxication, so it is worth being careful with.

japanese_cocktail.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
japanese_cocktail.description: One of the few cocktails definitely invented by Jerry Thomas and published in his 1862 book. It's thought to honor the first Japanese diplomatic mission to the US in 1860, which stayed in New York near Thomas's bar. Cognac, almond orgeat and bitters make a smooth, nutty, aromatic digestif, though there's nothing Japanese in it.
japanese_cocktail.creator: Jerry Thomas

japanese_highball.instructions: Fill a chilled glass with ice, add the whisky, stir 13 turns, top up with sparkling water and give it one or two more turns of the bar spoon.
japanese_highball.description: The whisky-and-soda highball went mainstream in Japan in the 1950s through Suntory's Torys bar chain, and the 2008 Kakubin Highball campaign brought it back into fashion. Japanese bartenders turned the simplest of drinks into a ritual: a chilled glass, crystal-clear ice, a precise number of stirs and the most highly carbonated water possible. It is drunk with food instead of beer, in izakayas for example.

japanese_slipper.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
japanese_slipper.description: Jean-Paul Bourguignon created the cocktail in 1984 at Mietta's restaurant in Melbourne. Equal parts Midori, Cointreau and lemon make a sweet-and-sour drink the colour of pale jade. It became one of the calling cards of 1980s Australian bartending and one of the few classics in which Midori tastes genuinely balanced.
japanese_slipper.creator: Jean-Paul Bourguignon (Mietta's)

jasmine.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
jasmine.description: Paul Harrington created the Jasmine around 1990 in California and later included it in his book Cocktail: The Drinks Bible for the 21st Century. Despite the name, there is no jasmine in it: the drink tastes like grapefruit juice, although it is made from gin, Campari, Cointreau and lemon. It was one of the early "new classics".
jasmine.creator: Paul Harrington

jello_shots.instructions: Dissolve the gelatin in hot water, let cool, add the vodka, pour into small cups and chill until set.
jello_shots.description: Jello shots are fruit gelatin mixed with vodka and set in small cups. They were popularized on American college campuses; the idea goes back to 19th-century recipes for punch jelly. They're treacherous because you can barely taste the alcohol.

jet_pilot.instructions: Flash blend with crushed ice and pour into a glass.
jet_pilot.description: The Jet Pilot is a version of Donn Beach's Test Pilot from The Luau restaurant in Los Angeles in the late 1950s. Three rums, cinnamon, grapefruit and falernum with a dash of absinthe make a powerful, spicy tiki drink of the jet age.
jet_pilot.creator: The Luau restaurant

juliet_and_romeo.instructions: Muddle the cucumber with salt and mint, add the rest, shake with ice and strain.
juliet_and_romeo.description: Toby Maloney created this cocktail for The Violet Hour in Chicago. Cucumber, mint, and drops of rose water and Angostura on a mint leaf turn a gin sour into a highly aromatic, garden-fresh drink.
juliet_and_romeo.garnish: mint leaf with drops of rose water and bitters
juliet_and_romeo.creator: Toby Maloney (The Violet Hour)

jungle_bird.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over fresh ice.
jungle_bird.description: The Jungle Bird was the signature welcome drink at the Aviary Bar of the Kuala Lumpur Hilton in 1978. It was nearly forgotten until renaissance bartenders revived it in the 2000s, swapping in dark blackstrap rum. Bitter Campari in a tropical rum drink is a bold combination that made it a bridge between tiki and Italian aperitivi.
jungle_bird.creator: Jeffrey Ong (Kuala Lumpur Hilton)

jungle_juice.instructions: Mix everything in a large container with ice and fruit.
jungle_juice.description: Jungle Juice is an American college party punch made in huge containers from vodka, rum and fruit juices. The name, so the story goes, came from WWII soldiers who mixed alcohol with whatever they could find. There is no recipe — just the principle of "lots of it, and sweet".

kalashnikov.instructions: Rest a lemon slice on the shot glass, half coated in sugar and half in coffee; drink the vodka and bite the lemon.
kalashnikov.description: The Kalashnikov shot is popular in bars in Russia and Eastern Europe: vodka topped with a lemon slice sprinkled with sugar and ground coffee. The lemon and coffee after the sip smooth out the alcohol. A similar serve with cognac is known as the Nikolashka.
kalashnikov.garnish: lemon slice with sugar and coffee

kalimotxo.instructions: Pour equal parts wine and cola into a glass with ice.
kalimotxo.description: Kalimotxo is a Basque drink of red wine and cola. According to the popular story, at a 1972 festival in Algorta, vendors discovered the wine they'd bought had gone off and saved it by mixing it with cola. The drink became a symbol of Spanish fiestas and youth culture; in the Czech Republic and other countries it goes by other names.

kamikaze.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into shot glasses or a cocktail glass.
kamikaze.description: The Kamikaze became popular in American bars in the 1970s; one legend ties it to a US military base in postwar Japan. Essentially it's a vodka Margarita without the salt, or a "Cosmopolitan without the cranberry". It's most often served as a party shooter, though it's also good as a sour in a glass.

karsk.instructions: Traditionally: place a coin in the bottom of a cup, pour in coffee until it can no longer be seen, then add spirit until the coin becomes visible again.
karsk.description: Karsk is a Scandinavian folk drink of weak coffee and moonshine, traditional in Trøndelag, Norway. It is known for its tongue-in-cheek measuring method: a coin is placed at the bottom, coffee is poured until it disappears, and spirit is added until it can be seen again.

kentucky_buck.instructions: Muddle the strawberry, shake with bourbon, juice and syrup, strain over ice and top up with ginger beer.
kentucky_buck.description: Erick Castro, who later opened Polite Provisions in San Diego, created the Kentucky Buck in the late 2000s. Strawberry, lemon, bourbon and ginger beer make a summer long drink in which the berry plays nicely with bourbon's vanilla.
kentucky_buck.creator: Erick Castro

kentucky_mule.instructions: Pour the bourbon and juice into an ice-filled mug and top up with ginger beer.
kentucky_mule.description: The Kentucky Mule is a bourbon version of the Moscow Mule that caught on with the American whiskey boom of the 2000s and 2010s. Caramel-and-vanilla bourbon makes it warmer and richer than the vodka original. It is served in the same copper mug; sometimes a couple of dashes of Angostura or a mint sprig are added, bringing it closer to a julep.

kioki_coffee.instructions: Pour the liqueur and brandy into a mug and top up with hot coffee.
kioki_coffee.description: Kioki Coffee is hot coffee with coffee liqueur and brandy (it is in TheCocktailDB). A sweet, aromatic and simple after-dinner drink. Similar to Jamaican Coffee, but with brandy instead of rum.

kir_royale.instructions: Pour the liqueur into a flute and top up with chilled champagne.
kir_royale.description: The classic Kir, white Burgundy Aligoté with blackcurrant liqueur, is named after Félix Kir, a priest, Resistance hero and mayor of Dijon who served it to guests to promote local products. The Kir Royale is the festive version made with champagne. A simple, elegant aperitif with a deep ruby colour.
kir_royale.creator: Félix Kir

last_word.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
last_word.description: The Last Word was first served at the Detroit Athletic Club around 1915 and, after decades of obscurity, was revived by Seattle bartender Murray Stenson in 2004. Equal parts of four bold ingredients strike a remarkable balance: the herbal power of Chartreuse is offset by cherry maraschino and tart lime. The drink spawned a whole family of twists, including the Paper Plane and the Naked and Famous.
last_word.creator: Detroit Athletic Club

lava_flow.instructions: Muddle the strawberries in the bottom of the glass; separately blend the rest with ice and pour on top so the strawberry "flows" up like lava.
lava_flow.description: The Lava Flow is a Hawaiian resort cocktail: strawberry purée at the bottom rises through the white coconut-banana mix like volcanic lava. A creamy, sweet and very showy alternative to the Piña Colada.

leap_year.description: Harry Craddock created the Leap Year for the February 29, 1928 celebrations at the Savoy and claimed it had prompted more marriage proposals than any other cocktail. Gin, Grand Marnier, vermouth and a dash of lemon — orangey and herbal.
leap_year.creator: Harry Craddock

lemon_drop_martini.instructions: Sugar-rim the glass; shake with ice and strain.
lemon_drop_martini.description: The Lemon Drop appeared in the 1970s at Norman Hobday's Henry Africa's in San Francisco, considered one of the first fern-and-Tiffany-lamp "singles bars". The name refers to the popular lemon hard candies. It is a sweet-and-sour cocktail with a sugar rim, much like a grown-up lemonade.
lemon_drop_martini.creator: Norman Jay Hobday (Henry Africa's)

lemon_drop_shot.instructions: Drink the chilled vodka and follow with a sugar-dipped lemon wedge.
lemon_drop_shot.description: The shot version of the Lemon Drop: ice-cold citrus vodka followed by a sugared lemon wedge. It tastes like a lemon hard candy; sometimes the shot is mixed with lemon juice and syrup right in the shaker.

lemon_lime_bitters.instructions: Soak the ice with bitters, then top up with soda and cordial.
lemon_lime_bitters.description: LLB is the signature soft drink of Australian pubs: lemon-lime soda, lime cordial and a generous dose of Angostura, which turns the drink pink. Refreshing, sweet and spiced.

lillet_tonic.instructions: Pour the Lillet over ice, top up with tonic and add fruit.
lillet_tonic.description: The Lillet Tonic became popular in the 2010s thanks to a campaign by the Lillet brand. A white wine aperitif from Bordeaux with a citrusy, floral character plus bitter tonic makes a light, lower-alcohol alternative to the G&T.
lillet_tonic.creator: Lillet

lime_rickey.instructions: Pour the juice and syrup over ice and top up with soda.
lime_rickey.description: The non-alcoholic Rickey was a hit at American soda fountains in the early 20th century. Lime, sugar and soda make the simplest of refreshers; in New England a raspberry syrup version (Raspberry Lime Rickey) is popular.

limonada_suica.instructions: Briefly blend the lime with water and sugar (no more than 10 seconds, to avoid bitterness), strain, add condensed milk and blend again.
limonada_suica.description: 'Swiss lemonade' is a Brazilian drink that has nothing to do with Switzerland: whole limes blended skin and all, with sweetened condensed milk. The result is creamy, refreshing and sweet-tart.

limonana.instructions: Blend everything until it reaches a sorbet-like consistency.
limonana.description: Limonana (limon + nana, "lemon" and "mint") is a frozen mint lemonade popular in the Middle East. Blended with ice to a slush, it is bright green and a lifesaver in the heat.

limoncello_spritz.instructions: Pour limoncello over ice, top up with prosecco and soda and stir gently.
limoncello_spritz.description: The Limoncello Spritz is a modern variation on the Venetian spritz using the southern Italian lemon liqueur from Sorrento and Amalfi. It became popular in the 2010s as a sweeter, more citrusy alternative to the Aperol Spritz. Light, sunny and aromatic; best with a good limoncello that is not too sweet, plus fresh mint or basil.
limoncello_spritz.garnish: lemon slice, basil or mint sprig

lions_tail.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
lions_tail.description: The recipe was printed in London's "Café Royal Cocktail Book" (1937); the name is probably linked to the expression "twisting the lion's tail" — provoking the British. Jamaican allspice liqueur gives the bourbon sour spicy notes of clove, cinnamon and nutmeg. It was revived in the 2000s along with the return of allspice dram to the market.

little_italy.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
little_italy.description: Audrey Saunders named this Manhattan with the artichoke amaro Cynar after New York's Italian neighbourhood. Cynar adds earthy bitterness and herbal depth, making the drink an excellent digestif.
little_italy.creator: Audrey Saunders (Pegu Club)

loch_lomond.description: Named after Scotland's largest loch: Scotch, honeyed herbal Drambuie and dry vermouth. Drier than a Rusty Nail and lighter thanks to the vermouth; it is in TheCocktailDB.

long_island_iced_tea.instructions: Pour everything except the cola into an ice-filled glass, stir and top up with cola (for the tea colour).
long_island_iced_tea.description: Robert Butt claimed he invented the drink in 1972 at the Oak Beach Inn on Long Island for a triple sec contest. Another story dates it to Prohibition, when a mix of spirits was disguised as iced tea. Five spirits with lemon and cola really do look like tea, and the sweetness masks the alcohol, which makes the drink deceptively strong.
long_island_iced_tea.creator: Robert "Rosebud" Butt (Oak Beach Inn, by his own account)

lucien_gaudin.description: The cocktail is named after Lucien Gaudin, the French fencer and Olympic champion of the 1920s. It's an elegant Negroni variation: dry vermouth and Cointreau make it drier and more citrusy.

lunchbox.instructions: Mix the beer with the orange juice, drop in a shot of amaretto and drink in one go.
lunchbox.description: The Lunchbox is a "bomb" shot for people who don't like beer: orange juice softens it, and amaretto makes it taste like an orange cookie. Popular in American college bars.

lychee_martini.description: The Lychee Martini became popular in the 1990s at Asian restaurants and fusion bars in the US. The floral, fruity flavor of lychee with neutral vodka makes a light, fragrant, very evening-friendly cocktail.

lynchburg_lemonade.instructions: Shake whiskey, liqueur, juice and syrup, strain over ice and top up with lemonade.
lynchburg_lemonade.description: The drink was created around 1980 by Tony Mason, a restaurant owner in Huntsville, Alabama; the name refers to Lynchburg, the town where Jack Daniel's is made. Mason later sued Jack Daniel's for using the recipe in its advertising. Sweet, citrusy and very summery.
lynchburg_lemonade.creator: Tony Mason

mad_dog.instructions: Pour the vodka, slowly sink the raspberry syrup to the bottom and add a drop of Tabasco.
mad_dog.description: Wściekły pies ('mad dog') is a popular Polish shot: vodka, raspberry syrup and Tabasco. The drops of sauce settle at the boundary between the layers like 'rabid foam'. It is also well known in Russian bars.

madras.instructions: Pour into an ice-filled glass and stir.
madras.description: The Madras belongs to the cranberry family of vodka highballs alongside the Cape Codder and the Sea Breeze. The name probably refers to the brightly checked madras cotton from the Indian city of Chennai, the drink being just as red and orange. Tart, fruity and refreshing, it is handy for brunch and large groups.

mai_tai.instructions: Shake with ice and pour over crushed ice; garnish with mint and a spent lime half.
mai_tai.description: Trader Vic claimed he invented the Mai Tai in 1944 at his Oakland restaurant; Tahitian guests who tried it exclaimed "Maita'i roa ae!" — "excellent!". His rival Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber) laid claim to an earlier, similar recipe. A true Mai Tai is not a sweet fruit punch but a complex rum sour with almond and orange, and an icon of tiki culture.
mai_tai.creator: Victor "Trader Vic" Bergeron

mamie_taylor.instructions: Pour Scotch and juice into an ice-filled glass and top up with ginger beer.
mamie_taylor.description: The drink is named after Broadway opera singer Mamie Taylor, who, according to legend, asked for "something light" after a boat trip in 1899. In the early 20th century the Mamie Taylor was hugely popular in America, long before the Moscow Mule came along. Scotch, lime and ginger make a simple, refreshing, slightly smoky highball.

manhattan.instructions: Stir all ingredients with ice in a mixing glass and strain into a chilled glass.
manhattan.description: The Manhattan appeared in New York in the 1870s–80s; the popular story about Jennie Churchill's banquet at the Manhattan Club is almost certainly invented, but the neighborhood's name stuck. It was one of the first cocktails in which vermouth became a full-fledged ingredient rather than an accent. The classic is made with rye, which is drier and spicier than bourbon; versions with dry vermouth are called a Dry Manhattan, and with equal parts of both vermouths, a Perfect Manhattan.

marconi_wireless.description: A cocktail from Hugo Ensslin's 1916 book, named after Guglielmo Marconi's wireless telegraph. Essentially it is a Manhattan made with apple brandy: appley, sweet and warming.
marconi_wireless.creator: Hugo Ensslin

margarita.instructions: Rim half the glass with salt; shake the ingredients with ice and strain.
margarita.description: The best-known tequila cocktail. There are at least a dozen origin stories — from a bar in Tijuana to a party thrown by socialite Margaret Sames in Acapulco — but in essence the Margarita is a Mexican take on the old-fashioned 'daisy' (margarita is Spanish for daisy). The salt rim lifts the citrus and softens the spirit. It is served frozen, on the rocks or straight up, as well as in fruit variations.

martinez.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
martinez.description: The Martinez is considered the direct ancestor of the Martini: the recipe appeared in American bartending manuals of the 1880s, and its origin is credited either to Jerry Thomas in San Francisco or to the town of Martinez, California. Essentially it is a Manhattan made with gin — equal parts spirit and sweet vermouth plus a touch of maraschino. It is noticeably softer and sweeter than a Dry Martini and shows well what cocktails were like before the fashion for 'dry'.

mary_pickford.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
mary_pickford.description: Named after silent film star Mary Pickford, the cocktail was created in Prohibition-era Havana and is credited to bartenders Eddie Woelke or Fred Kaufman. It's said to have been invented during a visit to Cuba by Pickford and her husband Douglas Fairbanks, though there's no reliable evidence of this. A delicate pink, sweet and fruity cocktail.
mary_pickford.creator: Eddie Woelke or Fred Kaufman

matador.description: A simple mix of tequila, pineapple and lime, first printed in the late 1930s. Pineapple juice gives a pleasant foam when shaken, and its flavor pairs well with grassy tequila. A great pineapple take on the Margarita without orange liqueur. It is often served on the rocks in an old fashioned glass, sometimes with a chili-salt rim.

matcha_tonic.instructions: Whisk the matcha with water, pour the tonic over ice and gently float the matcha on top.
matcha_tonic.description: Matcha tonic is a modern café trend and a relative of the espresso tonic: Japanese matcha green tea layered over bitter tonic. Grassy, energising and very photogenic thanks to its green gradient.

mauresque.instructions: Pour the pastis and orgeat, top up with ice-cold water and add ice.
mauresque.description: The Mauresque is pastis with orgeat almond syrup, popular in the south of France. The sweet almond softens the anise. Its family includes the Perroquet (with mint syrup), the Tomate (with grenadine) and the Rourou (with strawberry).

medusa_shot.instructions: Layer over a spoon: coconut liqueur, Cointreau, blue curaçao; drip Baileys on top so it curdles into a "jellyfish".
medusa_shot.description: The Medusa is a showy shot from Russian bars: clear and blue layers of orange and coconut liqueurs into which cream liqueur is dripped, curdling into jellyfish tentacles. It is downed in one through a straw or straight from the glass.

melon_ball.instructions: Build in a glass with ice and stir.
melon_ball.description: A 1980s highball riding the wave of Midori's popularity: melon liqueur, vodka and orange juice. Greenish, sweet and fruity, it is often served as a shot too. The name plays on melon balls scooped out with a melon baller.

metropolitan.description: The Metropolitan is a 19th-century "brandy Manhattan" known from the books of George Kappeler and others. Cognac instead of rye makes the drink softer, fruitier and rounder.

mexican_candy_shot.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a shot glass rimmed with chili salt.
mexican_candy_shot.description: This shot mimics the flavor of Mexican chili watermelon candies: tequila, watermelon liqueur, lime and a drop of hot sauce in a glass rimmed with Tajín. Sweet, spicy and salty all at once.

mexican_coffee.instructions: Pour the tequila and liqueur into a mug, top up with coffee and garnish with cream and cinnamon.
mexican_coffee.description: Hot coffee with tequila and coffee liqueur — a Mexican take on Irish Coffee. The cinnamon nods to traditional café de olla, brewed in a clay pot with cane sugar and spices.

mexican_firing_squad.instructions: Shake with ice, strain over fresh ice and top with a splash of soda if desired.
mexican_firing_squad.description: Charles Baker described this cocktail in The Gentleman's Companion (1939), recalling a 1937 visit to La Cucaracha bar in Mexico City. Tequila, lime, pomegranate grenadine and a generous dose of Angostura give a sweet-and-sour, spicy and very balanced flavour. One of the oldest documented tequila cocktails.
mexican_firing_squad.creator: La Cucaracha bar

mexican_flag.instructions: Layer over a spoon: grenadine, crème de menthe, tequila.
mexican_flag.description: A layered shot in the colors of the Mexican flag: red grenadine, green crème de menthe and clear tequila. Not to be confused with the Bandera — three separate shot glasses of lime, tequila and sangrita.

mexican_martini.instructions: Shake with ice and serve in a glass, with the remainder in the shaker on the side.
mexican_martini.description: The Mexican Martini is a local classic in Austin, Texas: essentially a Margarita with orange juice and olive brine, served in a martini glass. Traditionally, the rest of the drink is left with the guest in the shaker so they can top themselves up.

mezcal_mule.instructions: Muddle the cucumber with the syrup, add the mezcal, juice and purée, shake with ice, strain over ice and top up with ginger beer.
mezcal_mule.description: Jim Meehan created this cocktail at PDT, the New York speakeasy, in the late 2000s. From the Moscow Mule it keeps the idea of ginger and lime, while smoky mezcal, cucumber and passion fruit add layers. It is often garnished with a pinch of chili to highlight the spice. A good first encounter with mezcal for those wary of its smoke.
mezcal_mule.creator: Jim Meehan (PDT)

miami_vice.instructions: Blend a Piña Colada and a Strawberry Daiquiri separately (half the rum in each) and pour them in layers into one glass.
miami_vice.description: The Miami Vice is a resort two-in-one: half the glass is a Piña Colada, the other half a Strawberry Daiquiri. It's named after the 1980s TV series. The bright red-and-white layers make it one of the most photogenic beach drinks.

michelada.instructions: Rim the glass with chili salt; combine the lime juice and sauces in the glass, add ice and top up with cold beer.
michelada.description: The Michelada is a Mexican beer cocktail known in many regional variations, from a simple chelada with lime and salt to versions with tomato juice or Clamato. The name is explained in various ways, for example from "mi chela helada", "my cold beer". It is a favourite hot-day drink and a famous hangover cure, a kind of beer Bloody Mary.

midori_sour.instructions: Pour everything except the soda into a glass with ice, stir and top up with soda.
midori_sour.description: The Japanese melon liqueur Midori was launched in the US in 1978 at a party at New York's Studio 54, right after the filming of Saturday Night Fever. The sour made with it became one of the signature drinks of the disco era. Bright green, sweet and melony, it shines with fresh citrus rather than sour mix.

milano_torino.description: The Milano-Torino is the original mix of Milanese Campari and Turinese vermouth, served at Caffè Campari in the 19th century. It gave rise to the Americano (with soda) and the Negroni (with gin).
milano_torino.creator: Gaspare Campari

milk_punch.instructions: Combine the spirits, tea, citrus and sugar, pour into hot milk, let it curdle and strain through cloth until clear.
milk_punch.description: The first recorded recipe for clarified milk punch belongs to Mary Rockett (1711). The acid curdles the milk, and the curds filter the drink, making it clear and silky and allowing it to keep for months. The technique came back into fashion in the 2010s.
milk_punch.creator: Mary Rockett (first recorded recipe)

mimosa.instructions: Pour chilled juice into a flute and top up with Champagne.
mimosa.description: The Mimosa is often credited to Frank Meier of the Ritz in Paris around 1925, while its British twin, the Buck's Fizz, was created at London's Buck's Club in 1921 (with more Champagne). It's named after the mimosa flower, which resembles the bright yellow drink. Today it's a brunch essential.
mimosa.creator: Frank Meier (Ritz, by one account)

mind_eraser.instructions: Pour the coffee liqueur over ice, layer the vodka on top and top up with soda; drink in one go through a straw.
mind_eraser.description: The Mind Eraser is a layered shooter in a rocks glass: coffee liqueur, vodka and soda, downed in one go through a straw. Essentially a Black Russian with soda, built for speed.

mini_beer.instructions: Pour the Licor 43 and carefully layer the cream "foam" on top.
mini_beer.description: This shot looks like a tiny glass of beer: golden vanilla-citrus Licor 43 topped with a cream "head." Popular in the Netherlands, Belgium and Spain, it's often ordered for photos, since from a distance it's almost indistinguishable from the real thing.

mint_julep.instructions: Gently muddle the mint with the syrup, add bourbon and crushed ice, stir until the glass frosts, then top with a mound of ice.
mint_julep.description: Juleps have been known in the American South since the late 18th century, originally as a morning tonic. Since 1938 the Mint Julep has been the official drink of the Kentucky Derby, where more than a hundred thousand are served over two days. It is traditionally served in a silver or pewter cup that frosts over, with a bunch of mint placed right by the straw so the aroma reaches the nose with every sip.

missionarys_downfall.instructions: Blend everything with a small scoop of crushed ice and pour into a glass.
missionarys_downfall.description: An early Donn Beach cocktail from the 1940s: a frozen "smoothie" of rum, pineapple, mint, lime and honey with a touch of peach liqueur. The name is classic tiki irony: even a missionary couldn't resist. It is one of the most refreshing tiki drinks, bright green from the mint.
missionarys_downfall.creator: Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber)

mojito.instructions: Gently muddle the mint with sugar and lime juice, add rum and crushed ice, stir and top up with soda.
mojito.description: The Mojito's ancestor is thought to be El Draque, a mix of rough rum, sugar, lime and mint that, according to legend, was drunk by Francis Drake's sailors. The modern version took shape in Havana by the 1930s, and La Bodeguita del Medio turned it into a tourist icon (along with a line attributed to Hemingway). Don't grind the mint; just press it lightly so it doesn't turn bitter.

monaco.instructions: Pour the grenadine into the glass, then the lemonade and beer.
monaco.description: The Monaco is a French bistro drink: a panaché (beer with lemonade) with grenadine, which tints it red. Sweet and low in alcohol, it's a summer café favorite.

monkey_gland.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
monkey_gland.description: Harry MacElhone invented the drink in the 1920s at Harry's New York Bar and named it after the notorious experiments of surgeon Serge Voronoff, who grafted monkey gland tissue onto men for 'rejuvenation'. Orange juice, grenadine and a dash of absinthe make it fruity, with a mysterious anise note.
monkey_gland.creator: Harry MacElhone

monte_carlo.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
monte_carlo.description: The Monte Carlo was described by David Embury in 1948: essentially a Manhattan with Bénédictine in place of vermouth. The honeyed herbal liqueur makes the whiskey smooth, spicy and aromatic; it is a close relative of the Old Fashioned.

morning_glory_fizz.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice, strain and top up with soda.
morning_glory_fizz.description: A morning fizz from 1880s American bartending manuals, intended to "restore" the drinker after a party. Scotch, citrus, egg white and a drop of absinthe with soda make a frothy, refreshing and surprisingly complex drink.

moscow_mule.instructions: Pour the vodka and lime juice into a mug with ice and top up with ginger beer.
moscow_mule.description: Despite its name, the Moscow Mule was an American marketing project: in 1941 John Martin, who was promoting the then little-known Smirnoff vodka, and Jack Morgan, owner of the Cock 'n' Bull bar and a ginger beer producer, decided to help each other out. According to one version, the copper mugs came from an acquaintance who couldn't sell them. Martin photographed bartenders holding a mug and a bottle of Smirnoff — and that is how vodka entered American cocktail culture.
moscow_mule.creator: John Martin, Jack Morgan

mudslide.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over ice (or blend with ice cream).
mudslide.description: The Mudslide was born in the 1970s at the Wreck Bar in the Cayman Islands when a guest asked for a White Russian and there was no cream — Baileys was used instead. The cocktail later became famous in its frozen version with ice cream. Dessert-like, creamy, with coffee and chocolate notes.
mudslide.creator: Wreck Bar (Rum Point Club)

mulata_daisy.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chocolate-rimmed glass.
mulata_daisy.description: A mid-20th-century Cuban cocktail revived in the 2000s at bartending competitions. Rum, chocolate liqueur and anise-vanilla Galliano with lime make a surprisingly fresh chocolate sour.

mulled_wine.instructions: Heat the wine with the spices, orange and honey until almost boiling (do not boil), steep for 10 minutes and serve.
mulled_wine.description: Hot spiced wine was drunk as far back as ancient Rome, and medieval Europe knew it as hippocras. The German name Glühwein ("glowing wine") comes from the tradition of heating wine with red-hot iron. Today it is a symbol of the Christmas markets of Germany, Austria and Scandinavia (where its relative is called glögg) and a favorite winter drink in Russia. The main rule is never to let it boil, so the aroma doesn't evaporate.

naked_and_famous.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
naked_and_famous.description: Joaquín Simó created this drink at Death & Co in New York in 2011, describing it as 'the love child of a Last Word and a Paper Plane, conceived in the Mexican highlands'. Smoky mezcal, honeyed, herbal yellow Chartreuse and Aperol add up to a complex yet remarkably balanced flavor. It is one of the best entry points into the world of mezcal.
naked_and_famous.creator: Joaquín Simó (Death & Co)

navy_grog.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over a crushed-ice cone with a hole for the straw.
navy_grog.description: Donn Beach created the Navy Grog around 1941 as a tiki reimagining of naval grog — rum diluted with water. Three rums, honey, grapefruit and lime make it one of the most balanced tiki drinks. It was Richard Nixon's favorite cocktail at Trader Vic's restaurants; the famous presentation is over an 'ice cone' with a straw running through it.
navy_grog.creator: Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber)

negroni.instructions: Build in a rocks glass over ice and stir (or stir in a mixing glass and strain over fresh ice).
negroni.description: The best-known story has it that around 1919, at Caffè Casoni in Florence, Count Camillo Negroni asked for a stronger Americano, and the bartender swapped the soda for gin. Equal parts make the recipe easy to remember and endlessly adaptable: the Negroni gave rise to the Boulevardier, the Negroni Sbagliato and dozens of modern twists. It is the benchmark Italian aperitivo, bitter, sweet and herbal all at once, and Negroni Week is held in its honour every year.
negroni.creator: Count Camillo Negroni (according to legend), bartender Fosco Scarselli

negroni_sbagliato.instructions: Pour the Campari and vermouth over ice, top up with prosecco and stir gently.
negroni_sbagliato.description: The name translates as "mistaken Negroni": according to legend, in 1972 Mirko Stocchetto at Milan's Bar Basso grabbed sparkling wine instead of gin by mistake. The mistake was a happy one, producing a light, bubbly take on the Negroni. A global wave of interest followed a viral 2022 video in which actress Emma D'Arcy named it her favorite drink.
negroni_sbagliato.creator: Mirko Stocchetto (Bar Basso)

negus.instructions: Mix port with hot water, sugar and lemon, and dust with nutmeg.
negus.description: Negus is named after Colonel Francis Negus, who, according to legend, suggested in the 1720s diluting hot port with water to calm a heated argument. It later became a popular drink at balls and even children's parties.
negus.creator: Colonel Francis Negus

new_york_sour.instructions: Shake the whiskey, juice, syrup and egg white, strain over ice and gently float the wine on top over a bar spoon so it forms a layer.
new_york_sour.description: Despite its name, this sour probably appeared in Chicago in the 1880s and was first called the Continental Sour or Southern Whiskey Sour. A layer of red wine over a Whiskey Sour looks striking and adds a tannic, fruity note. Today it is one of the most photogenic classics.

nikolashka.instructions: Drink the cognac and follow it with a lemon slice sprinkled with sugar and ground coffee.
nikolashka.description: Nikolashka is a Russian way of serving cognac: knocked back in one go and chased with lemon, sugar and coffee. Legend links it to Emperor Nicholas II, though there is no documentary evidence; it is also known in Germany under the same name.

nojito_watermelon.instructions: Blend the watermelon, strain, shake with lime, syrup and mint, strain over ice and top up with soda.
nojito_watermelon.description: The Watermelon Cooler is a summer alcohol-free drink of fresh watermelon juice with lime and mint, close to the Mexican agua fresca de sandía. Light, sweet and very refreshing.

nuclear_daiquiri.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
nuclear_daiquiri.description: Gregor de Gruyther created the Nuclear Daiquiri in the mid-2000s at LAB bar in London. Overproof Jamaican white rum and green Chartreuse, both over 55% ABV, make it very potent, while falernum and lime keep it balanced. The vivid green color hints at the "radioactive" name.
nuclear_daiquiri.creator: Gregor de Gruyther (LAB)

nui_nui.instructions: Flash blend with crushed ice and pour into a glass.
nui_nui.description: The Nui Nui ("big" in Hawaiian) is a spiced Donn Beach tiki drink with cinnamon, vanilla and allspice. It is like a "Christmas" Daiquiri over crushed ice. The recipe long remained a secret and was reconstructed from the notes of Donn's bartenders.
nui_nui.creator: Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber)

nutty_irishman.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over ice (or add to hot coffee).
nutty_irishman.description: Irish cream liqueur and hazelnut Frangelico with milk: a dessert drink served on the rocks or poured into hot coffee. Nutty, creamy and very sweet.

oatmeal_cookie.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a shot glass.
oatmeal_cookie.description: A shot that tastes remarkably like an oatmeal raisin cookie with cinnamon: butterscotch, cream, Jägermeister and cinnamon. Listed on TheCocktailDB; popular in American bars.

oaxaca_old_fashioned.instructions: Stir with ice in a mixing glass, strain over a large cube and flame an orange peel over the glass.
oaxaca_old_fashioned.description: Phil Ward created the drink in 2007 at Death & Co in New York, and it did much to introduce mezcal to American bartenders. It applies the Old Fashioned template to agave spirits: aged tequila brings softness and vanilla, a little mezcal adds smoke. Ward later opened Mayahuel, a bar devoted entirely to agave.
oaxaca_old_fashioned.creator: Phil Ward (Death & Co)

old_cuban.instructions: Shake the rum, lime, syrup, mint and bitters with ice, double strain into the glass and top up with champagne.
old_cuban.description: Audrey Saunders created the Old Cuban in 2001, before opening her Pegu Club. It is an elegant hybrid of the Mojito and the French 75: aged rum, mint, lime and Angostura, topped with champagne. The drink showed that rum could be the base of grown-up drinks, not just beach ones.
old_cuban.creator: Audrey Saunders

old_fashioned.instructions: Soak the sugar with bitters and water and muddle; add ice and whiskey and stir until chilled; express the oils from a citrus peel over the top.
old_fashioned.description: One of the oldest cocktails there is: the formula 'spirit, sugar, water and bitters' was the very definition of the word cocktail in the early 19th century. When bartenders began adding liqueurs and absinthe, patrons started asking for a drink made 'the old-fashioned way', and the name stuck. The Pendennis Club in Louisville is often called the birthplace of this particular version, but that is more legend than fact. The Old Fashioned is the benchmark for showing off an aged whiskey: sugar softens the spirit, bitters add spicy depth and orange peel brings aroma.

old_pal.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
old_pal.description: The Old Pal appeared in Harry MacElhone's ABC of Mixing Cocktails (1922) and is dedicated to New York Herald journalist William 'Sparrow' Robertson. It is the drier sibling of the Boulevardier: rye, dry vermouth and Campari in equal parts. Bitter, dry and spicy — for those who find the Negroni too sweet.
old_pal.creator: Harry MacElhone

orange_whip.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over ice.
orange_whip.description: The Orange Whip became famous thanks to The Blues Brothers (1980), where John Candy asks for "three orange whips". Vodka and rum with orange juice and cream taste like orange ice cream.

oyster_shooter.instructions: Place the oyster in a shot glass, add the vodka and spicy tomato mix; drink in one go.
oyster_shooter.description: The Oyster Shooter is a shot with a fresh oyster, vodka and a spicy Bloody Mary-style mix. Popular in American oyster bars and along the coast; there are versions with beer or sake instead of vodka.

painkiller.instructions: Shake with ice, pour over crushed ice and dust with nutmeg.
painkiller.description: The Painkiller was born in the 1970s at the Soggy Dollar Bar on Jost Van Dyke, a bar guests swam to from their yachts and paid with "wet dollars." It was created by Daphne Henderson; Pusser's rum later trademarked the name. It's a creamy tropical punch, a relative of the Piña Colada but with darker rum and the spice of nutmeg.
painkiller.creator: Daphne Henderson (Soggy Dollar Bar)

palmetto.description: The Palmetto is a "rum Manhattan" from "The Savoy Cocktail Book": aged rum and sweet vermouth in equal parts with orange bitters. The name comes from the palmetto palm, the state tree of South Carolina.

paloma.instructions: Build tequila, lime juice and a pinch of salt in a glass over ice and top up with grapefruit soda.
paloma.description: In Mexico itself, the Paloma is more popular than the Margarita. Its invention is often credited to Don Javier Delgado Corona, owner of La Capilla bar in the town of Tequila, but there is no solid evidence; its spread was helped by Squirt grapefruit soda, which arrived in Mexico in the 1950s. The name means 'dove'. It is a light, bittersweet-tart and very refreshing long drink with a pinch of salt.
paloma.garnish: lime or grapefruit wedge, salt rim (optional)

paper_plane.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
paper_plane.description: Sam Ross created the Paper Plane in 2008 for The Violet Hour in Chicago; the name comes from the M.I.A. song "Paper Planes". It is an equal-parts riff on the Last Word, where bourbon meets bittersweet orange Aperol and caramel-herbal Amaro Nonino. The result is both refreshing and complex, and it quickly became a modern classic.
paper_plane.creator: Sam Ross

paradise.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
paradise.description: The Paradise first appears in American bartending books of the 1910s and made it into "The Savoy Cocktail Book" of 1930. Apricot liqueur and orange juice make it soft, sunny and fruity, while the gin holds the backbone. A simple cocktail that appeals to those just getting to know the classics.

pastis.instructions: Pour the pastis, then ice-cold water (1:5), and only then add ice.
pastis.description: Pastis is the anise aperitif of Provence, created after absinthe was banned; Paul Ricard launched the Ricard brand in 1932. With water it turns cloudy and yellow, hence the nickname "le Jaune". An essential part of Marseille cafés and games of pétanque.
pastis.creator: Paul Ricard

pearl_diver.instructions: Blend with crushed ice and pour into the glass.
pearl_diver.description: A famous 1930s tiki drink by Donn Beach that long remained a mystery because of its secret "gardenia mix" of honey, butter and spices. The result is a velvety, honeyed and spiced rum drink, traditionally served in a tall glass of a distinctive shape.
pearl_diver.creator: Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber)

pegu_club.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
pegu_club.description: The cocktail is named after the Pegu Club, a British officers' club in Rangoon (Burma) where it was served in the 1920s. The recipe made it into The Savoy Cocktail Book and became known worldwide. In 2005 Audrey Saunders named her New York bar after it, a venue that played a huge role in the cocktail renaissance. It is a dry, citrusy, slightly bitter drink, close to the Gimlet.
pegu_club.creator: Pegu Club

penicillin.instructions: Shake everything except the peated whisky with ice and strain over ice; gently float the peated Scotch on top.
penicillin.description: Sam Ross created the Penicillin in 2005 at Milk & Honey, taking the Gold Rush as a base and adding ginger and Scotch. The finishing touch is a float of peated Islay whisky that hits the nose with smoke right away. The drink spread around the world and became perhaps the best-known creation of the cocktail renaissance; the name plays on its "medicinal" ginger-and-honey flavor.
penicillin.creator: Sam Ross (Milk & Honey)

periodista.description: The Periodista ("journalist") is a cocktail of Cuban origin that was especially embraced in Boston, where it became a local classic. Rum, orange and apricot liqueurs with lime make a fruity, lively sour.

pharisaer.instructions: Dissolve the sugar in the coffee, add the rum and spoon on a thick layer of cream; drink without stirring.
pharisaer.description: A North Frisian legend: in the 19th century on the island of Nordstrand, christening guests secretly drank coffee with rum hidden under a thick layer of cream so the pastor wouldn't notice. When he found them out, the pastor exclaimed, "Oh, you Pharisees!", and that's how the drink got its name.

pickleback.instructions: Drink a shot of whiskey and chase it with a shot of pickle brine.
pickleback.description: The Pickleback is whiskey with a pickle brine chaser, invented in 2006 at the Bushwick Country Club bar in Brooklyn. The brine instantly kills the burn of the alcohol. For Russians the idea is a familiar one: chasing with a sip of pickle brine.
pickleback.creator: Reggie Cunningham (Bushwick Country Club)

pimms_cup.instructions: Fill the glass with ice and fruit, add the Pimm's and top up with lemonade or ginger ale.
pimms_cup.description: James Pimm, owner of a London oyster bar, created a gin-based herbal and spiced "cup" in the 1820s–40s that was served with fruit. Today Pimm's is Britain's quintessential summer drink and an integral part of Wimbledon, where it is served by the hundreds of thousands of glasses. Cucumber, strawberries and mint are the obligatory "salad" in the glass.
pimms_cup.creator: James Pimm

pina_colada.instructions: Blend with crushed ice (or shake with ice) and serve in a tall glass.
pina_colada.description: The national drink of Puerto Rico. The Caribe Hilton claims bartender Ramón Marrero created the Piña Colada in 1954, after canned Coco López cream of coconut appeared; the Barrachina restaurant contests this in favor of Ramón Portas Mingot (1963). The name means 'strained pineapple'. Rupert Holmes's 1979 song made the drink synonymous with a beach holiday.
pina_colada.creator: Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero (Caribe Hilton)

pineapple_upside_down_shot.instructions: Shake the vodka with the juice, strain into a shot glass and gently pour the grenadine so it sinks to the bottom.
pineapple_upside_down_shot.description: This shot mimics the flavor of American pineapple upside-down cake: vanilla vodka and pineapple with grenadine settling to the bottom like caramel. Sweet and dessert-like.

pink_gin.instructions: Rinse the glass with Angostura (or add it), then pour in chilled gin or stir with ice.
pink_gin.description: Pink Gin was the drink of 19th-century Royal Navy officers: Angostura was used as a remedy for seasickness and stomach troubles, and gin made it more pleasant. A few drops of bitters tint the gin pale pink. Today "pink gin" also refers to sweet pink berry gins, but the classic is this dry, spicy mix.

pink_lady.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain.
pink_lady.description: According to one version, the Pink Lady is named after a 1911 Broadway musical. In the 1930s–50s it was a high-society 'ladies'' cocktail. The classic version with applejack, egg white and grenadine is frothy, pink and fruity.

pink_squirrel.instructions: Shake with ice and strain (or blend with vanilla ice cream).
pink_squirrel.description: The Pink Squirrel was created at Bryant's Cocktail Lounge in Milwaukee, one of the oldest cocktail bars in the US. Crème de noyaux, a liqueur made from apricot kernels, gives the drink its almond flavor and pink color. In Wisconsin, with its love of dessert ice cream drinks, it's often made with vanilla ice cream.
pink_squirrel.creator: Bryant's Cocktail Lounge

pisco_punch.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a glass.
pisco_punch.description: Pisco Punch made San Francisco's Bank Exchange saloon famous in the 1890s, where owner Duncan Nicol kept the recipe strictly secret — he took it to his grave. Pisco was shipped from Peru by sea during the Gold Rush, and the punch was hugely popular until Prohibition. Reconstructions use pineapple syrup, lemon and pisco — a soft, tropical, floral drink.
pisco_punch.creator: Duncan Nicol (Bank Exchange)

pisco_sour.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice; strain and dash bitters onto the foam.
pisco_sour.description: The Pisco Sour was created in the 1920s at Morris' Bar in Lima by American bartender Victor Morris and later refined by his protégés, who added egg white and bitters. Today it is Peru's national cocktail (the country even has an official Pisco Sour Day), though Chile disputes the claim to pisco and has its own version. Floral grape pisco, a dense foam and aromatic drops of Angostura make the drink instantly recognizable.
pisco_sour.garnish: drops of Angostura on the foam
pisco_sour.creator: Victor Vaughen Morris (Morris' Bar)

piscola.instructions: Pour the pisco over ice and top up with cola.
piscola.description: The Piscola is Chile's national highball: pisco and cola. It is ordered in every bar in the country, and in the Peru–Chile dispute over pisco it is perhaps Chile's most widespread argument.

planters_punch.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into an ice-filled glass.
planters_punch.description: A Jamaican punch known for its rhyming rule "one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak" (sour, sweet, strong and weak in a 1:2:3:4 ratio). The link to planters and to the Planter's Hotel in St. Louis is more legend than fact, but the punch appears in print as early as the 1870s. Myers's rum long promoted it as its signature drink. There are countless recipes; what they share is dark rum, citrus, sugar and spice.

poinsettia.instructions: Pour the juice and liqueur into a flute and top up with champagne.
poinsettia.description: The Poinsettia is named after the red Christmas flower and has become one of the top holiday cocktails in the US. Cranberry, orange liqueur and champagne — tart, berry-forward and very festive.

polish_martini.description: The Polish Martini, credited to Dick Bradsell, brings together Polish ingredients: bison grass vodka, Krupnik honey liqueur and apple juice. The result is a soft, honey-and-apple drink with an herbal aroma, a relative of the Szarlotka.
polish_martini.creator: Dick Bradsell

ponche_navideno.instructions: Simmer the fruit with cinnamon, hibiscus and sugar for 30–40 minutes and serve hot with pieces of fruit.
ponche_navideno.description: Ponche navideño is a hot Mexican Christmas punch made for the posadas festivities. Guava, tejocote, apples, cinnamon and cane sugar; for adults, rum or brandy is often added ("con piquete").

pornstar_martini.instructions: Shake everything except the prosecco with ice and strain into a glass; serve the prosecco on the side in a shot glass.
pornstar_martini.description: Douglas Ankrah, co-founder of London's famous LAB bar, created the drink in 2002 at Townhouse and originally called it the Maverick Martini. The provocative name, he said, reflected the drink's confident, sexy character. The shot of sparkling wine on the side can be sipped as a chaser or poured into the glass. Within fifteen years the Pornstar had become the UK's best-selling cocktail.
pornstar_martini.creator: Douglas Ankrah (Townhouse)

port_and_starboard.instructions: Pour the grenadine, then layer the crème de menthe on top over a bar spoon.
port_and_starboard.description: The name comes from the nautical terms port (red light) and starboard (green light). The two layers — grenadine and green crème de menthe — mirror the colors of a ship's navigation lights; listed in TheCocktailDB.

port_light.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain over ice.
port_light.description: A rare bourbon tiki drink from Hawaii's Kahala Hilton in the 1960s. It was served in glasses shaped like a ship's lantern — hence the name. Passion fruit and grenadine bring tropical sweetness, while bourbon provides a warm backbone.
port_light.creator: Kahala Hilton hotel

port_sangaree.instructions: Stir with ice, strain over ice and dust with nutmeg.
port_sangaree.description: The Sangaree is an 18th-century drink that gave its name to sangria: wine (often port or Madeira), sugar and nutmeg. A light, spiced, berry-tinged digestif.

porto_flip.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice; strain and dust with nutmeg.
porto_flip.description: Flips are one of the oldest families of mixed drinks: in the 17th and 18th centuries the name referred to a hot mix of ale, rum and sugar frothed with a red-hot poker. Later the flip became a cold drink and gained a whole egg or a yolk. The Porto Flip, made with port and cognac, is velvety, smooth and dessert-like, a good example of how wine works in cocktails.

porto_tonico.instructions: Pour the port over ice and top up with tonic.
porto_tonico.description: The Porto Tónico is a Portuguese summer aperitif served in every bar in Porto. White port, slightly sweet and nutty, pairs well with bitter tonic. It is a light alternative to the G&T, lower in alcohol and fruitier. It works well with mint or an orange slice, and dry white port makes the drink less sweet.

pousse_cafe.instructions: Layer one bar spoon at a time, strictly in order of decreasing density: from grenadine to cognac.
pousse_cafe.description: The Pousse-Café ("coffee pusher") is a 19th-century French digestif of several liqueurs layered in different colors. It's the forerunner of all layered shots, from the B-52 to the Hiroshima; recipes vary, but what matters is the order of density.

prairie_fire.instructions: Pour tequila into a shot glass and add Tabasco.
prairie_fire.description: Prairie Fire is a challenge shot of tequila and Tabasco. The heat of the sauce and the spirit hit at the same time; some bars offer 'levels' by the number of drops.

presbyterian.instructions: Pour the Scotch into a glass with ice and top up with ginger ale and soda.
presbyterian.description: The Press, or Presbyterian, is an old-fashioned highball of whisky, ginger ale and soda, known since the late 19th century. The name hints at the drink's respectability: it's light and low in alcohol, as if made for a strict congregation. Mixing ginger ale with soda makes it less sweet than a regular whisky-ginger.

prince_of_wales.instructions: Shake cognac, Bénédictine, bitters and sugar, strain and top up with Champagne.
prince_of_wales.description: The recipe is attributed to the future King Edward VII, back when he was still Prince of Wales. Cognac, Bénédictine and bitters topped with Champagne: a luxurious, spicy and festive drink, like a Champagne Cocktail on steroids.
prince_of_wales.creator: Edward VII (according to legend)

purple_hooter.instructions: Shake the vodka, liqueur and lime, strain and top up with soda.
purple_hooter.description: The Purple Hooter is a purple 1980s shot of vodka, raspberry liqueur and lime. Tart, berry-driven and light; it is also served as a long drink with plenty of soda.

pussyfoot.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain.
pussyfoot.description: One of the first documented non-alcoholic cocktails, named after William 'Pussyfoot' Johnson, an American temperance campaigner. The recipe is credited to Robert Vermeire of the 1920s London/Paris bartending world. Citrus, grenadine and egg yolk make a velvety, fruity drink.
pussyfoot.creator: Robert Vermeire (according to one version)

quarter_deck.description: The Quarter Deck, named for the officers' deck, is a rum and sherry cocktail from classic British drinks books (and TheCocktailDB). The sherry adds a nutty sweetness, the lime freshness.

queens_park_swizzle.instructions: Muddle the mint in the bottom of the glass, add the rum, juice and syrup, fill with crushed ice and churn with a swizzle stick; top with Angostura.
queens_park_swizzle.description: Swizzles are a Caribbean tradition of churning a drink with crushed ice using a special stick cut from a tree branch. This version appeared in the 1920s at the Queen's Park Hotel in Port of Spain, Trinidad, the home of Angostura. Trader Vic called it "the most delightful form of anesthesia given out today." The layers, green mint below and red bitters on top, make it very striking.
queens_park_swizzle.creator: Queen's Park Hotel

queimada.instructions: Combine the orujo with sugar, peel and beans in a clay bowl and ignite, stirring until some of the alcohol burns off; ladle into cups.
queimada.description: Queimada is a Galician fire ritual: orujo with sugar, lemon and coffee is set alight in a clay bowl while the host recites a 'spell' (conxuro) to ward off evil spirits. The drink becomes softer and sweeter as the alcohol burns off.

quentao.instructions: Caramelize the sugar, add the water, ginger and spices, simmer, then add the cachaça and heat through.
quentao.description: Quentão ("hot") is a Brazilian hot drink of cachaça, ginger and spices, a must at the June Festa Junina celebrations, which fall in the southern winter. Warming and very aromatic.

radler.instructions: Pour equal parts beer and lemonade into a glass.
radler.description: The Radler (German for "cyclist") is linked to Bavarian innkeeper Franz Kugler, who, according to legend, stretched his dwindling beer with lemonade for a crowd of cyclists in 1922. In Britain a similar drink is called a shandy. It's a light, refreshing and very low-alcohol beer cocktail.
radler.creator: Franz Xaver Kugler

ramos_gin_fizz.instructions: Dry shake hard and long, then shake with ice; strain into a glass and top up with soda so the foam rises above the rim.
ramos_gin_fizz.description: Henry Ramos invented this fizz in 1888 at his Imperial Cabinet Saloon in New Orleans. Legend has it the drink had to be shaken for 12 minutes, and Ramos kept a whole 'chain' of shaker boys on every shift. Cream, egg white and orange flower water create a soft, cloud-like foam that rises above the glass. It is one of the most labor-intensive classics — and one of the most hated by bartenders at rush hour.
ramos_gin_fizz.creator: Henry Charles Ramos

ranch_water.instructions: Pour the tequila and juice into a glass with ice and top up with sparkling water (or add the tequila and lime straight into the bottle of water).
ranch_water.description: Ranch Water is a Texan drink of unclear origin, associated with West Texas ranches of the mid-20th century. Tequila, lime and highly carbonated Mexican Topo Chico mineral water — no sugar, very dry and refreshing. In the 2020s it went viral across America, and canned ready-to-drink versions even appeared.

rattlesnake.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain.
rattlesnake.description: A recipe from The Savoy Cocktail Book: Craddock joked that it would "either cure rattlesnake bite, or kill rattlesnakes, or make you see them". In essence it is a rye Whiskey Sour with a dash of absinthe.

rebujito.instructions: Mix in a pitcher with ice and mint.
rebujito.description: The Rebujito is the signature drink of Andalusian fairs, especially Seville's April Fair, where it is drunk by the pitcher. Dry manzanilla sherry is mixed with sparkling lemonade and mint, making a light, refreshing, slightly salty citrus drink that lets you party all night.

red_eye.instructions: Pour tomato juice into a glass and top up with beer.
red_eye.description: The Red Eye is beer with tomato juice, popular as a hangover cure in Canada and the US Midwest; Tom Cruise's character drinks one in the film Cocktail. A relative of the Michelada, but without the lime and sauces.

red_hook.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
red_hook.description: Vincenzo Errico created the Red Hook in 2004 at Milk & Honey, naming it after the Brooklyn neighborhood. Bittersweet Punt e Mes vermouth and maraschino turn the Manhattan into a darker, cherry-tinged and spicier drink; it's the best known of the "Brooklyn neighborhood" cocktails.
red_hook.creator: Vincenzo Errico (Milk & Honey)

red_snapper_shot.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into shot glasses.
red_snapper_shot.description: A shot unrelated to the gin Bloody Mary of the same name: Canadian whisky, amaretto and cranberry in equal parts. Sweet, nutty and berry-like; listed in TheCocktailDB.

remember_the_maine.instructions: Rinse the glass with absinthe; stir the rest with ice and strain.
remember_the_maine.description: The recipe was described by gourmet and traveler Charles Baker in "The Gentleman's Companion" (1939), recalling an evening in Havana in 1933. The name refers to the rallying cry of the Spanish–American War after the battleship Maine exploded in Havana harbor in 1898. It is a Manhattan with cherry liqueur and absinthe: dark, aromatic and complex.
remember_the_maine.creator: Charles H. Baker

revolver.description: Jon Santer created the Revolver in 2004 at Bruno's in San Francisco. Bourbon with a splash of coffee liqueur and orange bitters — a simple yet deep cocktail reminiscent of coffee with orange zest.
revolver.creator: Jon Santer (Bruno's)

rob_roy.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
rob_roy.description: The Rob Roy is a Manhattan made with Scotch. It was created in New York in 1894, most commonly said to be at the Waldorf hotel bar, for the premiere of the operetta Rob Roy about the Scottish folk hero. Scotch brings malty and sometimes lightly smoky notes, so the drink comes out drier and earthier than the original.
rob_roy.creator: Waldorf Hotel bar

rock_shandy.instructions: Pour lemonade and soda over ice and add bitters.
rock_shandy.description: The Rock Shandy, popular in South Africa and Australia, is equal parts lemonade and soda water with a few dashes of Angostura. Less sweet than lemonade and spicy from the bitters; it's a common order for drivers and athletes.

rompope.instructions: Heat the milk with sugar and spices, whisk in the egg yolk, thicken, cool and add the rum.
rompope.description: Rompope is a Mexican eggnog, according to legend created by the nuns of the Santa Clara convent in Puebla in colonial times. Thick, creamy and vanilla-scented, it is drunk at Christmas and used in desserts.
rompope.creator: Nuns of the Santa Clara convent (according to legend)

rose_cocktail.description: The Rose is a 1920s Parisian aperitif attributed to Johnny Mitta of the Chatham Hotel. It is built on dry French vermouth with a little kirsch and raspberry syrup: pale pink, dry and low in alcohol. TheCocktailDB gives a different, gin-based version.
rose_cocktail.creator: Johnny Mitta (Chatham Hotel)

rosita.instructions: Stir with ice and strain over fresh ice.
rosita.description: The Rosita is a 'tequila Negroni' with two vermouths; the recipe appeared in American bartending guides of the 1970s and was popularized in the 2000s by Gary Regan. Aged tequila with vanilla notes pairs well with bitter Campari. Softer and more complex than a classic Negroni.

royal_bermuda_yacht_club.description: Named after the historic yacht club in Bermuda and recorded by Trader Vic in the 1940s. In essence it is a Daiquiri with falernum and curaçao: spiced, citrusy and elegant.

royal_flush.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into shot glasses.
royal_flush.description: The name refers to the poker hand and nods to Crown Royal. Canadian whisky, peach schnapps and cranberry make a sweet, berry-flavored shot that's especially popular in casinos.

royal_hawaiian.description: The signature cocktail of Honolulu's "Pink Palace," the Royal Hawaiian hotel, which opened in 1927. Gin with pineapple, lemon and almond orgeat: an early "tiki before tiki" that's light, tropical and smooth.
royal_hawaiian.creator: Royal Hawaiian Hotel

rudesheimer_kaffee.instructions: Flame the brandy with sugar in the cup while stirring, top up with coffee and finish with whipped cream and chocolate.
rudesheimer_kaffee.description: Rüdesheimer Kaffee was invented in 1957 by Hans Asbach, a brandy producer from the Rhine wine town. The brandy is flamed with sugar, topped with coffee and crowned with whipped cream; it is served in special porcelain cups.
rudesheimer_kaffee.creator: Hans Asbach

rum_milk_punch.instructions: Shake with ice, strain and dust with nutmeg.
rum_milk_punch.description: A rum version of milk punch, popular since the 18th century. Rum, milk, sugar and nutmeg make a light, creamy and spiced drink, close to eggnog but without the egg.

rum_punch.instructions: Shake with ice (or mix in a bowl) and dust with nutmeg.
rum_punch.description: Rum punch is one of the oldest mixed drinks: British sailors probably brought the word "punch" itself back from India in the 17th century. In Jamaica it is made by the rule "one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak". Every bar and every family has its own recipe.

rum_runner.instructions: Blend with crushed ice (or shake) and serve in a tall glass.
rum_runner.description: The cocktail appeared in the 1950s at the Holiday Isle bar in the Florida Keys, where, according to legend, the bartender urgently needed to use up surplus rum and liqueurs. The name refers to Prohibition-era rum smugglers who ran liquor across the Straits of Florida. Sweet, fruity and very much a vacation drink.
rum_runner.creator: Holiday Isle bar (Islamorada)

russian_spring_punch.instructions: Shake everything except the champagne with ice, strain into a glass over ice and top up with champagne.
russian_spring_punch.description: Another 1980s creation by Dick Bradsell, devised for a private club in London. The drink has nothing to do with Russia or spring: 'Russian' refers to the vodka, and 'spring punch' is a pun linked to champagne (spring also meaning a natural source of water). It is a vivid, berry-driven sparkling long drink, handy for festive groups.
russian_spring_punch.creator: Dick Bradsell

rusty_nail.instructions: Build in a rocks glass over ice and stir.
rusty_nail.description: The Rusty Nail is the simplest of pairings: Scotch and Drambuie, a Scottish whisky liqueur made with honey and herbs. Similar mixes were known from the 1930s, and the modern name stuck in the 1960s, when the drink was fashionable in New York and associated with Sinatra's Rat Pack. It is a sweet, warming digestif; the amount of Drambuie is usually adjusted to taste.

safe_sex_on_the_beach.instructions: Build in a glass with ice and stir.
safe_sex_on_the_beach.description: A non-alcoholic version of the popular long drink (sometimes called Safe Sex on the Beach): peach, orange and cranberry. Sweet, fruity and showing a pretty gradient if the cranberry is poured in last.

saint_clements.description: The name refers to the English nursery rhyme "Oranges and lemons, say the bells of St. Clement's." Orange juice with bitter lemon is a British non-alcoholic classic for pubs and family occasions.

sake_bomb.instructions: Lay two chopsticks across a glass of beer and rest a shot of sake on them; bang the table so the shot drops into the beer, then down it in one.
sake_bomb.description: The Sake Bomb is an American (not Japanese) sushi-bar tradition: a shot of sake balanced on chopsticks over beer drops in when the table is struck. It is often accompanied by a chorus of "Ichi, ni, san — sake bomb!".
