saketini.description: The Saketini is a martini with dry sake in place of vermouth, popular in Japanese restaurants and sushi bars in the West. Sake brings a soft rice and floral note, and cucumber slices underline the freshness. Proportions range from almost straight gin to equal parts.

salty_dog.instructions: Rim the glass with salt and pour the vodka and juice into the glass with ice.
salty_dog.description: The Salty Dog is a Greyhound with a salt rim that became popular in the 1950s; "salty dog" was slang for a sailor. The salt softens the bitterness of the grapefruit and brings out its sweetness. A simple, refreshing, very beachy highball. Made with gin, it is closer to the 1930s original and more herbal.

sambuca_con_la_mosca.instructions: Pour the sambuca, drop in three beans, ignite for a few seconds, extinguish and drink, chewing the beans.
sambuca_con_la_mosca.description: An Italian tradition: sambuca with three coffee beans — 'flies' — symbolizing health, happiness and prosperity. It is often set alight briefly to release the coffee aroma, then extinguished and drunk.

sangria.instructions: Combine wine, brandy, juice, syrup and fruit and let steep in the fridge for a few hours; serve over ice, topped with soda.
sangria.description: Sangria is a Spanish and Portuguese wine punch whose name comes from sangre, "blood", for its color. Mixtures of wine with fruit and spices have long existed, but sangria won worldwide fame after the 1964 World's Fair in New York. In the EU the name is protected: only a drink from Spain or Portugal can be called sangria. It's made by the pitcher for a crowd, and the recipe varies widely from home to home.

sangrita.instructions: Mix and chill; serve in a shot glass alongside tequila.
sangrita.description: Sangrita ("little blood") is a traditional Mexican chaser for tequila from Jalisco. It was originally made with Seville orange juice, pomegranate and chili; today it is usually made with tomato and orange juices. It is served in a separate shot glass — for example, as part of a Bandera.

saoco.instructions: Pour rum and coconut water over ice (traditionally straight into a coconut).
saoco.description: Saoco is one of the oldest Cuban drinks: rum with coconut water, traditionally poured right into a fresh coconut. It is mentioned as a drink of rural Cuba as early as the 19th century. Light, slightly salty and very refreshing.

saratoga.description: A cocktail from Jerry Thomas's book, named after the fashionable resort of Saratoga Springs. Cognac and rye with vermouth make it an ancestor of the Vieux Carré: warm, woody and gently spiced.
saratoga.creator: Jerry Thomas

satans_whiskers.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
satans_whiskers.description: A recipe from The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930) in two versions: 'straight' whiskers with Grand Marnier and 'curled' with orange curaçao. Five ingredients in equal parts make a rich, orange-forward take on the Bronx. Bright, complex and yet easy-drinking.

saturn.instructions: Flash-blend with crushed ice (or shake) and serve.
saturn.description: The Saturn was created by Californian bartender J. 'Popo' Galsini; in 1967 it won an international bartending competition. It is a rare gin-based tiki drink: passion fruit, falernum and orgeat give it a tropical flavor, while the gin keeps it light and fresh. It is often garnished with a ring of peel, like the planet's ring.
saturn.creator: J. 'Popo' Galsini

sazerac.instructions: Rinse a chilled glass with absinthe; in a mixing glass, dissolve the sugar with the bitters, add the whiskey and ice, stir and strain into the glass.
sazerac.description: The Sazerac is the emblem of New Orleans and has been the city's official cocktail since 2008. It takes its name from Sazerac de Forge et Fils cognac, served at the Sazerac Coffee House in the mid-19th century, when apothecary Antoine Peychaud also created the bitters the recipe is unthinkable without. After phylloxera wiped out French vineyards, the cognac was replaced with rye whiskey. Absinthe is used only to rinse the glass, yet it gives the drink its signature anise aroma.

sbiten.instructions: Dissolve the honey in water, add the spices, heat almost to a boil, steep for 10 minutes and strain.
sbiten.description: Sbiten is an old Russian hot drink of honey, water and spices, known since the 12th century; sbiten vendors sold it at fairs from copper samovars. It was the main warming winter drink before tea became widespread. Alcoholic versions exist, but classic sbiten is non-alcoholic.

scarlett_ohara.description: Named after the heroine of Gone with the Wind, the cocktail was promoted by the makers of Southern Comfort on the back of the film's 1939 release. The peachy, spiced liqueur with cranberry and lime makes a tart, berry-forward, light drink.

scofflaw.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
scofflaw.description: In 1924 a Boston newspaper ran a contest for a word describing those who flouted Prohibition, and 'scofflaw' won. Within weeks, Harry's New York Bar in Paris was already serving a cocktail of the same name. Rye whiskey, dry vermouth, lemon and grenadine give a fresh, lightly fruity flavor.
scofflaw.creator: Bartender Jock (Harry's New York Bar)

scorpion.instructions: Flash-blend with crushed ice and pour into a glass (or a communal bowl for a group).
scorpion.description: Trader Vic popularised the Scorpion in the 1940s; he recalled being inspired by a drink he had tried in Hawaii. The Scorpion Bowl, a huge communal bowl with long straws, became especially famous. Rum, brandy, orange and almond orgeat make a fruity but deceptively strong punch.
scorpion.creator: Trader Vic

screaming_orgasm.description: A creamy coffee shot from the 1980s with a provocative name: vodka, amaretto, coffee liqueur and cream liqueur. Sweet and dessert-like; there is also a version served in a glass over ice.

screwdriver.instructions: Pour the vodka into a glass with ice and top up with orange juice.
screwdriver.description: In 1949, Time magazine wrote about a new drink among American oil engineers in the Middle East, who supposedly stirred vodka and orange juice with a screwdriver. Whatever the truth, its simplicity made the Screwdriver one of the most popular drinks in the world. Freshly squeezed juice turns it from a college drink into a respectable brunch cocktail.

sea_breeze.instructions: Build in an ice-filled glass and stir.
sea_breeze.description: Early 1920s Sea Breezes were made with gin and grenadine, but the modern version took shape in the 1970s on the back of Ocean Spray's cranberry juice promotion. It is a simple, tart long drink, less sweet than Sex on the Beach. Relatives include the Bay Breeze with pineapple juice and the Cape Codder with cranberry alone.

seelbach.instructions: Pour the bourbon, Cointreau and bitters into a flute, stir and top up with champagne.
seelbach.description: The cocktail is named after the Seelbach Hotel in Louisville. In 1995 bartender Adam Seger presented it as a "lost 1917 recipe", and the story was repeated for decades until he admitted he had made it up. Legend aside, it is an excellent celebratory drink: bourbon, orange liqueur, a generous dose of bitters and champagne.
seelbach.creator: Adam Seger

seven_and_seven.instructions: Pour the whisky over ice and top up with the soda.
seven_and_seven.description: The 7 and 7 is an American highball of Seagram's 7 Crown whisky and 7 Up, especially popular in the 1970s. The name is built entirely on brands, but the formula is simple: a smooth Canadian blend and lemon-lime soda.

severnoe_siyanie.instructions: Pour vodka into a glass and top up with champagne (sometimes with a dash of lemon juice).
severnoe_siyanie.description: Severnoe Siyanie ('Northern Lights') is a legendary Soviet 'cocktail' of champagne and vodka (pure spirit in the original legend), associated with polar explorers and student parties. A simple and treacherous combination: the bubbles speed up the effect of the alcohol. Variations exist with lemon juice or cognac.

sex_on_the_beach.instructions: Build in a glass over ice and stir (or shake and strain over ice).
sex_on_the_beach.description: According to the common story, the drink was born in Florida in 1987: a peach schnapps producer held a bartender competition, and one Ted Pizio named his recipe after the main pleasures of spring break. It is a sweet, fruity long drink, related to the Sea Breeze and the Woo Woo. One of the great symbols of '80s cocktails'.

sgroppino.instructions: Whisk the sorbet with the vodka until creamy, slowly add the prosecco and pour.
sgroppino.description: The Sgroppino is a Venetian dessert drink of lemon sorbet, vodka and prosecco, served between courses or at the end of a meal. The name is linked to the dialect word sgropar, "to untie (a knot)", meaning to settle the stomach after eating. It is creamy, citrusy and sparkling all at once.

shanghai_cocktail.description: A cocktail from The Savoy Cocktail Book: Jamaican rum with lemon, grenadine and anise. The anise adds a spicy, licorice note unusual for rum sours. The name is a nod to the 1920s–30s fashion for Oriental exotica.

sherry_cobbler.instructions: Briefly shake the sherry, syrup and orange with ice, pour over crushed ice and garnish with fruit.
sherry_cobbler.description: The Sherry Cobbler was perhaps America's most popular mixed drink in the 1830s–40s; Dickens describes it in Martin Chuzzlewit. It was this drink that popularized the drinking straw — without one, sipping through crushed ice was awkward. Sherry, a little sugar and fruit on a mound of ice make a refreshing, low-proof summer drink.

sherry_flip.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice and strain.
sherry_flip.description: The Sherry Flip is a 19th-century classic: oloroso or cream sherry, egg and sugar. The nutty, dried-fruit notes of the sherry turn into a velvety dessert with less strength than a Brandy Flip.

shirley_temple.instructions: Pour ginger ale into an ice-filled glass and add grenadine.
shirley_temple.description: The best-known non-alcoholic cocktail is named after Shirley Temple, the child film star of the 1930s. Its origin is credited to Chasen's in Beverly Hills or to the Royal Hawaiian in Honolulu; the actress herself said she found the drink too sweet. The version with cola is called a Roy Rogers.

shrub_soda.instructions: Pour the shrub over ice and top up with soda.
shrub_soda.description: A shrub is a 'drinking vinegar': fruit steeped with sugar and vinegar, an old way of preserving the harvest. With soda it makes a sweet-tart, vibrant drink that bartenders use in both alcohol-free and alcoholic cocktails.

sidecar.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
sidecar.description: The Sidecar appeared just after World War I; Harry's New York Bar in Paris and Buck's Club in London both claim it, and legend says it was named after an officer who arrived at the bar in a motorcycle sidecar. It is a cognac take on the Brandy Crusta and a relative of the Margarita and the White Lady. A good Sidecar is dry, citrusy and shows off the fruitiness of the cognac.

siesta.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
siesta.description: Katie Stipe created the Siesta in 2006 at New York's Flatiron Lounge. Essentially it is a tequila Hemingway Daiquiri with Campari in place of maraschino. Bittersweet, grapefruity, fresh and aperitif-like, it is close in spirit to the Paloma. A good example of how Italian bitter pairs with agave — the same idea behind the Rosita.
siesta.creator: Katie Stipe (Flatiron Lounge)

singapore_sling.instructions: Shake all ingredients with ice and strain into a glass over ice.
singapore_sling.description: The drink is credited to Ngiam Tong Boon, bartender at the Long Bar of Singapore's Raffles Hotel, around 1915. Slings are an old family of 'spirit, sugar, water' drinks, but the Singapore version picked up pineapple, cherry, Bénédictine and grenadine. The original recipe was lost and has been reconstructed many times, so versions vary widely. For tourists at Raffles it is a must.
singapore_sling.creator: Ngiam Tong Boon (Raffles Hotel)

slippery_nipple.instructions: Pour the sambuca, then gently layer the cream liqueur on top over a bar spoon.
slippery_nipple.description: A 1980s layered shot of sambuca and cream liqueur; their different densities let them settle into two layers. The anise sweetness of sambuca is softened by creamy Baileys. A typical party shot with a provocative name. Sometimes a drop of grenadine is added at the bottom for a third layer, making the shot even more striking.

sloe_gin_fizz.instructions: Shake the liqueur, juice and syrup with ice, strain into the glass and top up with soda.
sloe_gin_fizz.description: Sloe gin is a British liqueur made from sloe berries steeped in gin with sugar. A fizz based on it was hugely popular in America in the early 20th century, and later, in the era of cheap imitations, came to be seen as a "girly" drink. With the return of quality sloe gins, the cocktail is back: tart, berry-driven, ruby-red and light.

smoky_martini.instructions: Rinse the glass with Scotch (or add it to the mixing glass), stir the gin with ice and strain.
smoky_martini.description: The Smoky Martini is a variation in which the vermouth is replaced by peated Scotch, sometimes used only as a rinse. Frank Sinatra is said to have liked it in a similar form. Gin stays front and center, while the whisky adds a smoky note.

snakebite.instructions: Pour equal parts lager and cider into a pint glass; add syrup for a Snakebite & Black.
snakebite.description: The Snakebite is a British mix of lager and cider, popular in student bars since the 1980s; with blackcurrant cordial it becomes a Snakebite & Black. It has a reputation as a treacherous drink, and some pubs refused to serve it. Sweetish, apple-and-malt and fizzy.

snaquiri.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a small glass.
snaquiri.description: The Snaquiri (snack + daiquiri) is a one-sip mini Daiquiri that bartenders around the world pour for each other as a greeting. Rum, lime and sugar in miniature: arguably the most "industry" shot there is.

snowball.instructions: Pour advocaat over ice, add lime and top up with lemonade, stirring gently.
snowball.description: The Snowball is a British Christmas drink made with advocaat, the Dutch egg liqueur, and lemonade, especially popular in the 1970s. Creamy and fizzy at once, it's associated with family holidays and is now enjoying a retro revival.

soju_yakult.instructions: Mix in equal parts with ice.
soju_yakult.description: A Korean party drink: soju, cultured Yakult and lemon-lime soda. Sweet, tangy and creamy, and very treacherous because you can barely taste the soju; it is often made by the pitcher for a group.

sol_y_sombra.instructions: Pour the brandy and anís into a glass (sometimes layered) and serve without ice.
sol_y_sombra.description: 'Sun and shade' is a Spanish drink of brandy and anís, named after the sunny and shaded stands of a bullring. In Andalusia and Castile it is traditionally drunk by workers as a morning warm-up or as a digestif.

somaek.instructions: Drop a shot of soju into beer (or mix roughly 3:7) and drink.
somaek.description: Somaek (soju + maekju, 'beer') is Korea's most popular 'bomb shot', a fixture of company dinners. There is a whole culture of flashy serves — with table-banging and chopstick 'tornadoes'.

southside.instructions: Shake with mint and ice, then double strain into a chilled glass.
southside.description: The Southside's origins are murky: it's linked variously to Chicago's South Side and Al Capone's gang, to the Southside Sportsmen's Club on Long Island, and to New York's famous "21" Club. Either way, it dates to Prohibition. In essence it's a gin Mojito without soda, or a Gimlet with mint: very fresh, herbal and easy-drinking.

spaghett.instructions: Drink a little beer from the bottle, then pour the Aperol and lemon juice straight into the neck.
spaghett.description: The Spaghett is a tongue-in-cheek "poor man's Aperol Spritz" that took off on the American internet in the late 2010s: Aperol and lemon poured straight into a bottle of light lager. The name plays on Aperol's Italian character. A bittersweet, citrusy beer that by the 2020s had even made it onto the menus of serious cocktail bars.

spanish_coffee.instructions: Rim the glass with sugar, flame the rum and triple sec in the glass until the sugar caramelizes, add the coffee liqueur and coffee, and top with cream.
spanish_coffee.description: Spanish Coffee is the signature drink of Huber's, Portland's oldest restaurant, where it's made tableside with a fiery show: the rum is set alight to caramelize the sugar on the rim. Sweet, coffee-rich and highly theatrical.
spanish_coffee.creator: Huber's Cafe

spicy_fifty.instructions: Shake with ice and the chili, then double strain into a chilled glass.
spicy_fifty.description: Famed London bartender Salvatore Calabrese created the Spicy Fifty in the 2000s for his bar 50 St James. Vanilla vodka, elderflower and honey make a soft, sweet base, while fresh chili adds a distinct burn. An example of how heat found its way into modern cocktails.
spicy_fifty.creator: Salvatore Calabrese

spritzer.instructions: Mix the wine and water (usually 1:1), with or without ice.
spritzer.description: The Spritzer is wine with sparkling water, a traditional drink in Austria and Hungary (fröccs), where there is a whole system of ratios, each with its own name. Known since the 19th century, it is the forerunner of the spritz.

st_germain_cocktail.instructions: Pour the liqueur over ice, top up with sparkling wine and soda, and stir gently.
st_germain_cocktail.description: St-Germain elderflower liqueur, launched by Robert Cooper in 2007, was used so often by bartenders that it earned the nickname "bartender's ketchup". The brand's signature drink, a spritz with sparkling wine and soda, is floral, light and very summery.
st_germain_cocktail.creator: Robert Cooper (St-Germain)

star_cocktail.description: The Star is a cocktail from American books of the 1880s: apple brandy and sweet vermouth in equal parts with bitters. Essentially an early version of the Marconi Wireless — a mellow, fruity and herbal drink.

stinger.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass (or over crushed ice).
stinger.description: The Stinger appeared in American high society in the early 20th century and was long regarded as a gentleman's digestif, drunk after dinner to aid digestion. It stayed fashionable right up to the 1950s, turning up in films and novels. Crème de menthe brings coolness, while cognac provides a fruity, woody backbone; served over crushed ice, the drink becomes lighter.

stone_sour.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over ice.
stone_sour.description: The Stone Sour, or California Sour, is any sour with orange juice added. It is most often made with bourbon or apricot brandy (the Apricot Stone Sour). Softer and fruitier than a regular Whiskey Sour.

strawberry_lemonade.instructions: Muddle strawberries with syrup and juice, shake with ice, strain over ice and top up with soda.
strawberry_lemonade.description: Strawberry (pink) lemonade is one of the most popular summer soft drinks. Muddled strawberries bring color and sweetness, lemon brings acidity; raspberry, watermelon and peach lemonades follow the same template.

suffering_bastard.instructions: Shake the gin, brandy, lime and bitters with ice, strain into an ice-filled glass and top up with ginger beer.
suffering_bastard.description: Joe Scialom, bartender at Shepheard's Hotel in Cairo, created the drink in 1942 as a hangover cure for British officers during the North African campaign. It is said to have been sent by the jug to the front at El Alamein. Gin and brandy with lime and ginger beer make a refreshing, invigorating long drink, later adopted by tiki culture.
suffering_bastard.creator: Joe Scialom (Shepheard's Hotel)

switchel.instructions: Mix the vinegar, honey and ginger, top up with water and serve over ice.
switchel.description: Switchel, or "haymaker's punch", was drunk by American farmers in the 18th and 19th centuries during haying: water with vinegar, honey or molasses and ginger quenches thirst well. In the 2010s it returned as a trendy functional drink.

szarlotka.instructions: Pour the vodka over ice and top up with apple juice.
szarlotka.description: Szarlotka is a Polish highball of Żubrówka (vodka infused with bison grass) and apple juice, also known as a Tatanka. It is named after szarlotka apple pie, which it tastes like: coumarin from the grass gives vanilla and almond notes reminiscent of cinnamon. A simple drink and a great favorite in Poland.

tarkhun.instructions: Muddle the tarragon with the syrup and juice, shake with ice, strain over ice and top up with soda.
tarkhun.description: Tarragon lemonade was invented by Tbilisi pharmacist Mitrofan Lagidze in 1887, and in the USSR the green Tarkhun became one of the most recognisable sodas. The homemade version with fresh tarragon is herbal, with light anise notes, and very refreshing.
tarkhun.creator: Mitrofan Lagidze

tennessee_mud.instructions: Pour whiskey and amaretto into a mug, top up with coffee and finish with cream.
tennessee_mud.description: Hot coffee with Tennessee whiskey and amaretto under a cap of cream (listed on TheCocktailDB). Softer than Irish coffee thanks to amaretto's almond sweetness. The name is a joke about the drink's "muddy" color and the state of Tennessee.

tequila_mockingbird.description: The name is a pun on Harper Lee's novel To Kill a Mockingbird (1960). There are many recipes; the classic version is tequila with crème de menthe and lime, a minty, refreshing sour.

tequila_shot.instructions: Lick salt from your hand, drink the tequila and bite into a lime wedge.
tequila_shot.description: The salt–tequila–lime ritual is most popular outside Mexico: salt and citrus tame the harshness of young tequila. In Mexico itself, good tequila is more often sipped slowly, served with sangrita.

tequila_slammer.instructions: Cover the shot glass with your palm, slam it on the table so the drink foams up, and drink at once.
tequila_slammer.description: The Tequila Slammer (Tequila Boom) is a shot of tequila with a fizzy mixer: the glass is covered with a palm and slammed on the table, then the foaming mix is downed in one. A bar hit of the 1980s–90s in Europe and Russia.

tequila_sunrise.instructions: Pour the tequila and juice into a glass with ice, then gently pour in the grenadine so it sinks to the bottom.
tequila_sunrise.description: The original 1930s Tequila Sunrise from the Arizona Biltmore hotel was made with crème de cassis and soda. The modern version with orange juice and grenadine was created in the early 1970s by bartenders Bobby Lozoff and Billy Rice at The Trident in Sausalito. It was made famous by the Rolling Stones, who drank it on their 1972 tour, and by the Eagles song. As the grenadine sinks, it creates the "sunrise" gradient.
tequila_sunrise.creator: Bobby Lozoff and Billy Rice (The Trident)

terremoto.instructions: Put a scoop of ice cream in a glass, pour wine over it and add grenadine or a dash of Fernet.
terremoto.description: Terremoto ('Earthquake') is a Chilean folk drink of sweet pipeño wine with pineapple ice cream. Legend ties it to Santiago's El Hoyo bar and German journalists who came to cover the 1985 earthquake. They say one glass leaves you 'shaking', and the second is called the 'aftershock'.
terremoto.creator: El Hoyo bar (according to legend)

test_pilot.instructions: Flash blend with crushed ice and pour into the glass.
test_pilot.description: Donn Beach's Test Pilot (around 1941) is the forerunner of the Jet Pilot. Rum, Cointreau, falernum and lime with a few drops of absinthe make a dry, spicy tiki drink, less fruity than most of the genre.
test_pilot.creator: Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber)

thai_iced_tea.instructions: Brew the tea, sweeten with condensed milk, chill and pour over ice, then top with cream.
thai_iced_tea.description: Thai iced tea (cha yen) is strong spiced black tea with condensed milk and cream, poured over ice. It's recognizable by its bright orange color and sweet, creamy taste, and it's perfect for cooling the heat of Thai food.

three_dots_and_a_dash.instructions: Flash blend with crushed ice and pour into a glass.
three_dots_and_a_dash.description: Another Donn Beach creation from the World War II era: "three dots and a dash" is the letter V (for Victory) in Morse code. The garnish echoes the symbol: three cherries and a pineapple chunk on a pick. Rhum agricole, falernum and allspice create a spicy, complex tropical flavor; a well-known Chicago tiki bar is named after it.
three_dots_and_a_dash.garnish: three cherries and a pineapple chunk on a pick
three_dots_and_a_dash.creator: Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber)

three_wise_men.instructions: Pour the three whiskies into one shot glass.
three_wise_men.description: Three Wise Men is a shot whose three whiskies are chosen for the names on their labels: Jack, Johnnie and Jim. Add Jose Cuervo tequila and you get the Four Horsemen. The taste is strong whiskey, no frills.

ti_punch.instructions: Squeeze a lime disc into the glass, add syrup and rum, stir; ice optional.
ti_punch.description: Ti' Punch (from the Creole "petit punch", "little punch") is the everyday aperitif of the French Antilles, Martinique and Guadeloupe. It's built on rhum agricole, distilled from fresh sugarcane juice, with a vivid grassy, vegetal character. Traditionally guests mix their own: the host sets out rum, lime and syrup, and everyone follows the rule "chacun prépare sa propre mort", "each prepares their own death".

tia_mia.instructions: Shake with ice and pour over crushed ice.
tia_mia.description: Ivy Mix created the Tia Mia by splitting the rum in a Mai Tai with mezcal. Agave smoke and funky Jamaican rum sit beautifully on almond orgeat; the drink became the calling card of her Brooklyn bar Leyenda.
tia_mia.creator: Ivy Mix

tinto_de_verano.instructions: Pour the wine and lemonade into an ice-filled glass.
tinto_de_verano.description: "Summer red" is an everyday Spanish drink that many Spaniards drink more often than sangria. It is associated with the Venta de Vargas in Córdoba in the early 20th century. Red wine with sparkling lemonade (or soda) makes a light, refreshing drink for hot days and tapas.
tinto_de_verano.creator: Venta de Vargas (according to legend)

tipperary.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
tipperary.description: The recipe was published by Hugo Ensslin in 1916 and named after the Irish county; the song "It's a Long Way to Tipperary" was popular at the time. It's a relative of the Bijou, but made with Irish whiskey: a smooth malty spirit, sweet vermouth and herbal Chartreuse. One of the few classic stirred cocktails built on Irish whiskey.
tipperary.creator: Hugo Ensslin

toasted_almond.description: The Toasted Almond is a 1970s American dessert cocktail: amaretto, coffee liqueur and cream. It tastes like almond ice cream with coffee; with vodka added it becomes a Roasted Toasted Almond.

tom_collins.instructions: Pour the gin, juice and syrup into an ice-filled glass, top up with soda and stir.
tom_collins.description: The Collins traces its lineage to John Collins, a waiter at London's Limmer's club in the early 19th century, while the name 'Tom' took hold after the New York hoax of 1874, when people were told that a certain Tom Collins was spreading rumors about them in the bar next door. Essentially it is a gin lemonade: a sour lengthened with soda. The IBA lists it today as the John Collins; the tall Collins glass is named after it.

tommys_margarita.instructions: Shake with ice and strain over fresh ice.
tommys_margarita.description: In the early 1990s, Julio Bermejo at his family's Tommy's restaurant in San Francisco swapped the orange liqueur in the Margarita for agave syrup. The result was a "cleaner" drink that put the flavor of good 100% agave tequila front and center. Bermejo became one of the world's leading tequila evangelists, and Tommy's a cult destination for agave lovers.
tommys_margarita.creator: Julio Bermejo (Tommy's Mexican Restaurant)

toreador.description: The Toreador, from the Café Royal Cocktail Book (1937), is one of the first published tequila cocktails. Apricot liqueur and lime make it a fruity sour — a forerunner of sorts to the Margarita.

toronto.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
toronto.description: A recipe called the Fernet Cocktail appeared in Robert Vermeire's 1922 book with a note that it was popular in Toronto; David Embury later cemented the name Toronto. It's a rye Old Fashioned with a spoonful of Fernet-Branca, which adds minty bitterness. A dark, herbal digestif.

treacle.instructions: Stir the rum, syrup and bitters with ice, strain over ice and float the apple juice on top.
treacle.description: Dick Bradsell created the Treacle in the 1990s: a rum Old Fashioned with a float of apple juice. That simple touch adds fruity freshness to dark rum, and the drink became one of London's modern classics.
treacle.creator: Dick Bradsell

trident.description: Robert Hess created the Trident, inspired by the Negroni but with a Nordic character: caraway-spiced Scandinavian aquavit, fino sherry and artichoke Cynar. A dry, spicy and bitter aperitif.
trident.creator: Robert Hess

trinidad_sour.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
trinidad_sour.description: Giuseppe González created the drink in 2009 at Clover Club in Brooklyn, flipping the usual proportions: Angostura bitters is the base here, and the whiskey is just an accent. Despite the bitters' nearly 45% ABV, orgeat and lemon make it remarkably balanced: spicy, nutty, with a bitter finish. It became a symbol of the renaissance era's daring.
trinidad_sour.creator: Giuseppe González (Clover Club)

turf_cocktail.description: The Turf (as in the racetrack) is an early 20th-century cocktail from the early martini family, close to the Tuxedo: gin, dry vermouth, maraschino, absinthe and bitters. Dry, aromatic and complex.

tuxedo.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
tuxedo.description: Named after the club in the country enclave of Tuxedo Park near New York, which also gave its name to the tuxedo. It is one of the early forms of the martini: equal parts gin and dry vermouth with dashes of maraschino and absinthe. More aromatic and less dry than a modern Dry Martini.
tuxedo.creator: Tuxedo Club

twentieth_century.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
twentieth_century.description: The cocktail was published in the "Café Royal Cocktail Book" (1937) and named after the luxury 20th Century Limited train between New York and Chicago. Gin, Lillet and crème de cacao sounds like an odd combination, but with lemon it achieves a remarkable balance: fresh and citrusy with a light chocolate finish.
twentieth_century.creator: C. A. Tuck

vampiro.instructions: Combine everything except the soda in an ice-filled glass and top up with soda.
vampiro.description: The Vampiro is a Mexican cocktail from the state of Jalisco, essentially tequila mixed with sangrita — a spicy tomato-citrus juice traditionally served alongside tequila. The name comes from its blood-red color. Spicy, sweet-and-sour and salty all at once, it is Mexico's answer to the Bloody Mary.

vegas_bomb.instructions: Shake the whiskey, schnapps and juice, strain into a shot glass and drop it into a glass of energy drink.
vegas_bomb.description: A 'bomb' in the style of the Jägerbomb, but with a Royal Flush shot (Canadian whisky, peach schnapps, cranberry) dropped into an energy drink. Popular in Las Vegas bars and at parties.

vento.instructions: Dry shake, then shake with ice; strain over fresh ice.
vento.description: The Ve.n.to was created by Italian bartenders in the 2010s to present grappa in a modern format; the name nods to the Veneto region, grappa's homeland. The grape spirit, lemon and a honey-chamomile syrup make a soft, floral sour. It is a fine example of a national spirit being brought back into cocktail culture.

vermouth_cassis.instructions: Pour vermouth and cassis over ice and top up with soda.
vermouth_cassis.description: Vermouth Cassis is an early 20th-century French aperitif that Hemingway mentions in A Moveable Feast. Dry vermouth with blackcurrant liqueur and soda makes a light, berry-tinged highball.

vermut_con_sifon.instructions: Pour the vermouth over ice and top up with sparkling water; serve with an olive.
vermut_con_sifon.description: The Spanish tradition of "la hora del vermut" means having a vermouth before lunch on the weekend. The classic of Madrid and Barcelona vermuterías is red vermouth on ice with an olive and a splash from the siphon.

vesper.instructions: Shake with ice (as Bond insisted) or stir; strain into a chilled glass.
vesper.description: Ian Fleming invented the Vesper for his novel Casino Royale (1953): James Bond orders "three measures of Gordon's, one of vodka, half a measure of Kina Lillet" and names the drink after Vesper Lynd. The original Kina Lillet was more bitter than today's Lillet Blanc, so Cocchi Americano is sometimes used instead. It is a stronger, more citrusy relative of the Martini that became popular after the 2006 film.
vesper.creator: Ian Fleming

vieux_carre.instructions: Stir in a mixing glass with ice and strain over fresh ice.
vieux_carre.description: Created in the late 1930s by Walter Bergeron, head bartender at the Hotel Monteleone in New Orleans; the name means 'old square', the French name for the French Quarter. The recipe brings together the city's cultures: American rye, French cognac and Bénédictine, Italian vermouth and the local Peychaud's bitters. The result is rich, spicy and velvety — a more complex cousin of the Manhattan.
vieux_carre.creator: Walter Bergeron (Hotel Monteleone)

virgin_mule.instructions: Pour the lime juice over ice, top up with ginger beer and garnish with mint.
virgin_mule.description: An alcohol-free version of the Moscow Mule: spicy ginger beer, lime and mint in a copper mug. It keeps all the ritual and flavour of the original, just without the vodka, and is one of the most ordered mocktails.

virgin_paloma.instructions: Rim the glass with salt, combine the juices and syrup over ice and top up with soda.
virgin_paloma.description: The Virgin Paloma keeps the essentials — bitter grapefruit, lime and a pinch of salt — replacing the tequila with extra soda. A dry, grown-up-tasting non-alcoholic drink.

vodka_tonic.instructions: Pour the vodka into a glass with ice and top up with tonic.
vodka_tonic.description: The Vodka Tonic emerged as vodka spread through the West in the mid-20th century, as a more neutral alternative to the Gin and Tonic. Quinine tonic provides bitterness and bubbles, while vodka adds strength without botanical notes.

ward_eight.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
ward_eight.description: According to Boston legend, the Ward Eight was first mixed in 1898 at Locke-Ober to celebrate politician Martin Lomasney's election victory in the Eighth Ward. It is a Whiskey Sour with orange juice and grenadine, fruitier and softer than the original. One of Boston's signature historic cocktails.
ward_eight.creator: Locke-Ober Café (according to legend)

washington_apple_shot.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into shot glasses.
washington_apple_shot.description: A shot named after Washington State, famous for its apples: Canadian whisky, sour apple liqueur and cranberry. Sweet-tart and fruity; it's also served as a cocktail in a glass.

wassail.instructions: Heat the cider with spices and honey, add sherry or brandy, and serve from a communal bowl.
wassail.description: Wassail is a medieval English hot punch of cider or ale with spices and baked apples; the name comes from the Old English for 'be well'. It was drunk during the winter holidays while going from house to house singing ('wassailing') and blessing the apple orchards.

water_lily.description: Richie Boccato created the Water Lily as an equal-parts drink in the spirit of the Last Word and the Corpse Reviver. Crème de violette tints it lilac and adds a floral aroma, while Cointreau and lemon make it bright and fresh.
water_lily.creator: Richie Boccato

whiskey_cola.instructions: Pour the whiskey into an ice-filled glass and top up with cola.
whiskey_cola.description: Whiskey and cola is one of the most ordered highballs in the world; bars often call it by the whiskey brand, as in "Jack and Coke". The caramel notes of cola pair easily with vanilla-rich bourbon, and a lemon or lime wedge freshens it up.

whiskey_daisy.instructions: Shake with ice, strain over crushed ice and add a splash of soda.
whiskey_daisy.description: The Daisy is a 19th-century cocktail family: spirit, citrus, liqueur (or syrup) and a little soda. It gave rise to the Sidecar and the Margarita. A Whiskey Daisy made with orange liqueur or yellow Chartreuse is fresh but full of character.

whiskey_ginger.instructions: Pour the whiskey into an ice-filled glass, top up with ginger ale and squeeze in the lime.
whiskey_ginger.description: Whiskey and ginger ale is a standard highball in many Irish bars (often with Jameson) and American pubs. The ginger highlights the smoothness of Irish whiskey, while the lime keeps the drink from getting cloying.

whiskey_smash.instructions: Muddle lemon wedges with mint and syrup in a shaker, add bourbon and ice, shake and strain over crushed ice.
whiskey_smash.description: Smashes are the younger siblings of juleps, known since the 1880s; the Whiskey Smash appears in the 1887 edition of Jerry Thomas's book. Dale DeGroff revived its popularity at New York's Rainbow Room by adding muddled lemon wedges. It is a fresh, minty, citrusy way to drink bourbon in summer.

whiskey_sour.instructions: If using egg white, dry shake first, then shake with ice; strain over fresh ice.
whiskey_sour.description: Sours are one of the oldest cocktail families, tracing back to naval punches, and the Whiskey Sour first appeared in print in Jerry Thomas's 1862 book. The spirit + citrus + sugar formula became the basis for hundreds of cocktails. Egg white is optional, but it adds a silky texture and a dense foam, often dotted with Angostura. The variation with a red wine float is called the New York Sour.

whisky_mac.instructions: Build in a glass (with or without ice) and stir.
whisky_mac.description: The Whisky Mac is a British winter drink of Scotch and ginger wine, according to legend invented by a Colonel Macdonald in the days of British India. The ginger warms and softens the whisky; it is traditionally drunk without ice on a cold day, say after fishing or shooting.

white_lady.instructions: Shake with ice (if using egg white, dry shake first) and strain into a chilled glass.
white_lady.description: An early version made with crème de menthe belongs to Harry MacElhone (1919), but the gin version published in Harry Craddock's "The Savoy Cocktail Book" in 1930 became the classic. Essentially it's a gin Sidecar: pale, dry and citrusy. Egg white came later, adding a lush white foam that lives up to the name.
white_lady.creator: Harry Craddock (gin version)

white_negroni.instructions: Stir with ice and strain over fresh ice.
white_negroni.description: British bartender Wayne Collins came up with the White Negroni in 2001 at the VinExpo wine fair in Bordeaux, when he had no Campari or vermouth on hand. He used French Lillet Blanc and Suze, a bitter gentian-root aperitif. The result was a pale, floral, bitter cocktail, the most popular of the "Negronis without the Negroni."
white_negroni.creator: Wayne Collins

white_russian.instructions: Pour the vodka and liqueur over ice, then gently float the cream on top (or stir lightly).
white_russian.description: The White Russian is a Black Russian with cream; the first mentions date to the mid-1960s. It became a cult drink thanks to the Coen brothers' film The Big Lebowski (1998), where the Dude drinks "Caucasians" in almost every scene. It is a creamy coffee dessert cocktail that many think of as a boozy latte.

wibble.description: Dick Bradsell created the Wibble in 1999 for Plymouth Gin. Two gins, regular and sloe, with grapefruit and blackberry make a berry-forward, bittersweet citrus cocktail; the name is British slang for "to wobble".
wibble.creator: Dick Bradsell

widows_kiss.instructions: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
widows_kiss.description: The recipe was published by George Kappeler in Modern American Drinks (1895). Apple brandy is combined with two 'monastic' liqueurs — Bénédictine and yellow Chartreuse. The result is a sweet, honeyed, herbal and deep digestif; Kappeler called it one of the best autumn drinks.
widows_kiss.creator: George Kappeler

wine_cooler.instructions: Pour wine over ice and top up with lemonade.
wine_cooler.description: The Wine Cooler is wine lengthened with soda and fruit; in the 1980s it was hugely popular in the US as a ready-to-drink bottled product. The homemade version is an easy way to turn wine into a light summer long drink.

woo_woo.instructions: Pour into a glass with ice and stir.
woo_woo.description: The Woo Woo is a 1980s long drink from the peach schnapps boom, a close relative of the Sex on the Beach (minus the orange juice). The name, according to one version, imitates party whoops. Sweet, fruity and simple; often served as shots. Unlike Sex on the Beach, there's no orange, so it's tarter and more berry-forward.

yellow_bird.instructions: Shake with ice and strain into a chilled glass.
yellow_bird.description: The Yellow Bird is a mid-20th-century Caribbean cocktail whose name is linked to the popular Haitian song "Yellow Bird". Vanilla-anise Galliano and orange liqueur turn a rum sour bright yellow and aromatic. It exists in many versions, often with added juices.

yorsh.instructions: Pour the vodka into a mug of beer (or drink the beer, chasing it with vodka).
yorsh.description: Yorsh is a Russian folk 'cocktail' of beer and vodka, known since pre-revolutionary times; according to one version, the name comes from the ruffe, a spiny fish, likened to the drink's prickly effect. It is considered one of the most treacherous combinations: the beer's carbonation speeds up alcohol absorption. It is a direct relative of the American Boilermaker.

zombie.instructions: Shake (or flash-blend) with crushed ice and pour into a glass.
zombie.description: Donn Beach created the Zombie in 1934 at his Hollywood bar — according to legend, for a hungover customer who needed to get through a business meeting. Built on three kinds of rum, it was so strong that the bar served no more than two per person. Donn kept the recipe secret, coding the ingredients, and the exact formula was only recovered by tiki historian Jeff Berry in 2007.
zombie.creator: Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber)
